Dynamic Minimax Regret Optimization
for Robust LLM Post-Training

Chengbo Zang Affiliation: Department of Electrical Engineering, Columbia University Email: cz2678@columbia.edu    Haoyu Dong Affiliation: Department of Electrical Engineering, Columbia University Affiliation: Department of Computer Science & Engineering, University of California, Santa Cruz Email: hd2573@columbia.edu    Mehmet Kerem Turkcan Affiliation: Department of Civil Engineering, Columbia University Email: mkt2126@columbia.edu    Gil Zussman Affiliation: Department of Electrical Engineering, Columbia University Email: gz2136@columbia.edu    Zoran Kostic Affiliation: Department of Electrical Engineering, Columbia University Email: zk2172@columbia.edu    Javad Ghaderi Affiliation: Department of Electrical Engineering, Columbia University Email: jg3465@columbia.edu
Abstract

Modern LLM training increasingly relies on heterogeneous data sources spanning different domains, tasks, preference distributions, and difficulty levels. We study dynamic minimax regret for group-distributionally robust LLM post-training under instantaneous mini-batch-only bandit feedback. The framework views the training as a two-player sampler-optimizer process: a sampler adaptively selects among data sources using bandit feedback, while an optimizer updates the model parameters using stochastic gradients from the selected source. We focus on the practically restrictive setting where source losses evolve with model training but historical data are not re-evaluated, requiring the sampler to track instantaneous worst-sources from stale partial feedback. We propose DUCB-OGD, a simple and scalable algorithm that couples a Discounted Upper-Confidence-Bound sampler with an Online Gradient Descent optimizer. The sampler maintains exponential moving average loss estimates and confidence radii based on discounted effective sample sizes, avoiding costly re-evaluation of past data or intrusive changes to standard training pipelines. For KK data sources and TT training steps, we prove that DUCB-OGD achieves a dynamic minimax regret of O~​(K1/4​T3/4)\tilde{O}(K^{1/4}T^{3/4}), which is optimal up to logarithmic factors for the undiscounted objective under our feedback model. Extensive experiments across supervised fine-tuning, preference optimization, and reinforcement learning show that DUCB-OGD integrates seamlessly into modern LLM training pipelines and improves worst-group robustness with negligible computational overhead compared with standard sampling baselines.

1 Introduction

Diverse data mixtures are central to modern Large Language Model (LLM) post-training. For example, supervised fine-tuning data may combine instruction-following, coding, mathematical reasoning, safety, and domain-specific examples; preference datasets may reflect different annotator populations or task families; and reinforcement learning objectives may expose the model to prompts whose rewards evolve unevenly during training (Ouyang et al., 2022; Rafailov et al., 2023; Schulman et al., 2017; Shao et al., 2024). As a result, post-training is not merely an average-loss minimization problem. A model can improve substantially on common or easy sources, while remaining weak on smaller, harder, or temporarily under-trained groups. This makes robust performance across data sources a central objective in LLM post-training. In practical deployment, worst-source robustness is a complementary and equally important criterion to the commonly reported mean performance, but often under-emphasized in aggregate evaluations.

Group-distributionally robust optimization (GDRO) provides a principled formulation for this goal by minimizing the worst-case expected loss over a predefined set of data sources (Duchi and Namkoong, 2021; Sagawa* et al., 2020; Oren et al., 2019). Informally, GDRO seeks model parameters that perform well on the most challenging source rather than the average performance across sources. However, the standard GDRO viewpoint is essentially static: robustness is typically evaluated with respect to the worst-performing source at the final or time-averaged solution, or determined in hindsight over the training trajectory (Zhang et al., 2023; Soma et al., 2025). This static benchmark does not fully capture the shift of the worst-performing source as the model evolves in LLM post-training. A robust algorithm should therefore track and respond to the evolving worst source, rather than optimize against a fixed source chosen in hindsight.

Recent work has shown that mixture proportions can strongly affect pretraining and post-training performance, motivating both offline mixture optimization and online adaptive sampling methods (Xie et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023; Ye et al., 2025; Corrado et al., 2025; Shin et al., 2025). Such mechanisms can be expensive or intrusive in large-scale post-training systems, where throughput, memory efficiency, and compatibility with distributed training libraries are critical. This creates a gap between the theoretical appeal of GDRO and the practical constraints of LLM post-training: we need adaptive algorithms that are robust, theoretically grounded, and lightweight enough to integrate into standard training pipelines relying on well-optimized deep learning libraries. We discuss related work in detail in Appendix A.

In this paper, we study dynamic minimax regret for group-distributionally robust LLM post-training under instantaneous mini-batch-only bandit feedback. The training trajectory can be naturally decomposed into a sampler, which selects a source using only its observed mini-batch loss, and an optimizer, which updates the model using the corresponding stochastic gradient. We propose DUCB-OGD, a simple algorithm that combines a Discounted Upper-Confidence-Bound (DUCB) (Garivier and Moulines, 2011) sampler with an Online Gradient Descent (OGD) (Hazan, 2016) optimizer. In contrast, while Zang et al. (2025) already study dynamic worst-source tracking, they refresh source-loss estimates by re-evaluating accumulated historical samples. Our replay-free formulation instead uses fresh mini-batches as unbiased stochastic estimates of population loss, adds no auxiliary model evaluations, and requires only O⁡(K)O(K) scalar state, at the cost of tracking unobserved sources from stale feedback. We show that this simple sampler-optimizer design achieves dynamic minimax regret of O~​(K1/4​T3/4)\tilde{O}(K^{1/4}T^{3/4}) for KK data sources over TT training steps, which is optimal for the undiscounted objective up to logarithmic factors under our feedback model.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

  1. 1.

    We formulate robust LLM post-training under instantaneous mini-batch-only feedback, where evolving source losses must be tracked from stale observations without historical replay or auxiliary model evaluations.

  2. 2.

    We propose DUCB-OGD, an efficient algorithm that combines DUCB sampling with OGD optimization, and prove that it achieves a dynamic minimax regret of O~​(K1/4​T3/4)\tilde{O}(K^{1/4}T^{3/4}), matching the optimal rate up to O⁡(log⁡T)O(\log T) factors for the undiscounted objective under our feedback model.

  3. 3.

    We evaluate the method across supervised fine-tuning, preference optimization, and reinforcement learning, showing improved worst-source robustness under negligible computational overhead against standard and heuristic sampling baselines.

2 Problem Setup

Let 𝕏\mathbb{X} be a data space with KK data sources indexed by [K]:={1,…,K}[K]:=\{1,\dots,K\}. Each source k∈[K]k\in[K] is associated with a distribution 𝒟k\mathcal{D}^{k} supported on 𝕏\mathbb{X}, and each query to source kk returns i.i.d. samples from 𝒟k\mathcal{D}^{k}. Let θ\theta be the learnable parameter from a parameter space 𝚯\mathbf{\Theta}. Let ℓ:𝚯×𝕏→ℝ\ell:\mathbf{\Theta}\times\mathbb{X}\to\mathbb{R} be a differentiable loss function. The expected loss of source kk at the model parameter θ\theta is defined as μk​(θ):=𝔼X∼𝒟k​[ℓ⁡(θ,X)]\mu^{k}(\theta):=\mathbb{E}_{X\sim\mathcal{D}^{k}}[\ell(\theta,X)]. A global minimax solution is any optimizer of the GDRO objective, i.e.,

θ⋆∈arg​minθ∈𝚯⁡maxk∈[K]​μk​(θ).\theta^{\star}\in\argmin_{\theta\in\mathbf{\Theta}}\max_{k\in[K]}\mu^{k}(\theta). (1)

This formulation captures a broad class of LLM post-training objectives through appropriate choices of the source distributions and loss functions as described in Tab. 1. Let πθ\pi_{\theta} be an LLM, and q,oq,o be a pair of prompt and response. Then πθ​(o|q)\pi_{\theta}(o|q) is the probability that the LLM generates the response oo given the prompt qq. In supervised fine-tuning (SFT), each source generates prompt-response pairs, and the loss is the negative log-likelihood of the target response (Ouyang et al., 2022). For direct preference optimization (DPO), let (o+,o−)(o^{+},o^{-}) denote a preferred and dispreferred response pair. Let pθBT​(o+≻o−|q)p_{\theta}^{\mathrm{BT}}(o^{+}\succ o^{-}|q) denote the Bradley-Terry probability (Rafailov et al., 2023; Bradley and Terry, 1952) that the model prefers o+o^{+} to o−o^{-}, and the loss is the negative Bradley-Terry preference probability. For reinforcement learning (RL), let r⁡(q,o)r(q,o) denote the reward assigned to the response oo for the prompt qq. Each source generates prompts, the model induces the response distribution, and the loss is the negative reward (Schulman et al., 2017; Shao et al., 2024). For simplicity, Tab. 1 presents these objectives at the sequence level, omitting token-wise factorization, reference-model regularization, and implementation-specific normalization terms.

We consider an iterative training algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A}, consisting of a sampler and an optimizer, that runs for TT steps. At each step t∈[T]t\in[T], the sampler specifies a distribution 𝒫t\mathcal{P}_{t} over the data-source indices [K][K]. A source kt∼𝒫tk_{t}\sim\mathcal{P}_{t} is then selected, and a mini-batch ℬt⊆𝕏kt\mathcal{B}_{t}\subseteq\mathbb{X}^{k_{t}} of i.i.d. samples is drawn from the corresponding distribution 𝒟kt\mathcal{D}^{k_{t}}. The model observes ℬt\mathcal{B}_{t} and calculates the empirical loss μ^kt​(θt,ℬt):=∑X∈ℬtℓ⁡(θt,X)/|ℬt|\hat{\mu}^{k_{t}}(\theta_{t};\mathcal{B}_{t}):=\sum_{X\in\mathcal{B}_{t}}\ell(\theta_{t},X)/|\mathcal{B}_{t}| based on the current model parameter θt\theta_{t}. Then the optimizer updates the parameter to obtain θt+1\theta_{t+1} for the next step. The sampler observes only μ^kt​(θt,ℬt)\hat{\mu}^{k_{t}}(\theta_{t};\mathcal{B}_{t}); it neither observes the current losses of unselected sources nor re-evaluates historical mini-batches. After TT steps, the algorithm generates a trajectory of data source indices and model parameters 𝒜T:={(kt,θt),t=1,…,T}\mathcal{A}_{T}:=\{(k_{t},\theta_{t}),t=1,\dots,T\}. Our goal is to evaluate this trajectory by how well it controls the adaptive sequence of maximum source-wise losses throughout the training. Following the notion of dynamic regret in online learning, the (undiscounted) dynamic minimax regret is defined as follows.

Definition 1 (Undiscounted Dynamic Minimax Regret).

Let θ⋆\theta^{\star} be the global minimax optimum in Eq. 1. The undiscounted dynamic minimax regret of an algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} after TT steps is defined as

R⁡(𝒜T):=∑t=1Tmaxk∈[K]⁡μk​(θt)−T​maxk∈[K]​μk​(θ⋆).R(\mathcal{A}_{T}):=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\max_{k\in[K]}~\mu^{k}(\theta_{t})-T\max_{k\in[K]}~\mu^{k}(\theta^{\star}). (2)

This definition compares the worst-case loss incurred by 𝒜T\mathcal{A}_{T} with the best achievable minimax loss. Crucially, the maximizing source in maxk⁡μk​(θt)\max_{k}\mu^{k}(\theta_{t}) may vary with tt, which makes the regret dynamic (Zang et al., 2025), i.e., at each step, it reflects the source that is currently under-performing, rather than a single fixed source chosen in hindsight (Zhang et al., 2023; Soma et al., 2025). To analyze the sampler-optimizer structure, we decompose the regret into an optimization component and a bandit component. The optimization component measures how well the optimizer competes with the minimax solution on the sampled sources. The bandit component measures how well the sampler tracks the instantaneous worst-performing source. We also introduce discount factors ρ,γ∈[0,1]\rho,\gamma\in[0,1] to emphasize recent observations, which is natural in post-training because source-wise losses evolve as the model changes.

Definition 2 (Optimization Regret and Dynamic Bandit Regret).

Let ρ,γ∈[0,1]\rho,\gamma\in[0,1]. The discounted optimization regret of an algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} after TT steps is defined as

Roρ​(𝒜T):=∑t=1TρT−t​(μkt​(θt)−μkt​(θ⋆)),R_{o}^{\rho}(\mathcal{A}_{T}):=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\rho^{T-t}\Big(\mu^{k_{t}}(\theta_{t})-\mu^{k_{t}}(\theta^{\star})\Big), (3)

and the discounted dynamic bandit regret is defined as

Rbγ​(𝒜T):=∑t=1TγT−t​(maxk∈[K]⁡μk​(θt)−μkt​(θt)).R_{b}^{\gamma}(\mathcal{A}_{T}):=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\gamma^{T-t}\Big(\max_{k\in[K]}\mu^{k}(\theta_{t})-\mu^{k_{t}}(\theta_{t})\Big). (4)

The optimization regret RoρR_{o}^{\rho} captures the loss incurred by following the optimizer trajectory instead of using the minimax solution on the sampled sources. The bandit regret RbγR_{b}^{\gamma} captures the loss incurred by sampling ktk_{t} instead of the instantaneous worst-performing source at time tt. The following decomposition connects these quantities to the original undiscounted regret. Its proof simply follows from the fact that maxk⁡μk​(θ)≥μkt​(θ)\max_{k}\mu^{k}(\theta)\geq\mu^{k_{t}}(\theta) for all θ\theta and tt and is provided in Appendix C.1.

Proposition 1 (Regret Decomposition).

Any trajectory 𝒜T\mathcal{A}_{T} satisfies R⁡(𝒜T)≤Ro1​(𝒜T)+Rb1​(𝒜T)R(\mathcal{A}_{T})\leq R_{o}^{1}(\mathcal{A}_{T})+R_{b}^{1}(\mathcal{A}_{T}).

Finally, we define the normalized discounted dynamic minimax regret as follows.

Definition 3 (Dynamic Minimax Regret).

For any ρ,γ∈[0,1]\rho,\gamma\in[0,1], the normalized (ρ,γ)(\rho,\gamma)-discounted dynamic minimax regret of an algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} after TT steps is defined as

Rρ,γ​(𝒜T):=TNT​(ρ)​Roρ​(𝒜T)+TNT​(γ)​Rbγ​(𝒜T),R^{\rho,\gamma}(\mathcal{A}_{T}):=\frac{T}{N_{T}(\rho)}R_{o}^{\rho}(\mathcal{A}_{T})+\frac{T}{N_{T}(\gamma)}R_{b}^{\gamma}(\mathcal{A}_{T}), (5)

where NT​(β):=∑t=1TβT−tN_{T}(\beta):=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\beta^{T-t} for any β∈[0,1]\beta\in[0,1].

The normalization converts each discounted sum to the scale of a length-TT horizon, making regret bounds comparable across choices of ρ\rho and γ\gamma. Here, ρ\rho and γ\gamma separately discount the optimization and bandit components, whereas β\beta will be selected by the analyses. When ρ=γ=1\rho=\gamma=1, the normalized regret reduces to the undiscounted sampler-optimizer decomposition, and by Proposition 1, R⁡(𝒜T)≤R1,1​(𝒜T)R(\mathcal{A}_{T})\leq R^{1,1}(\mathcal{A}_{T}). For ρ,γ<1\rho,\gamma<1, the discounted statistics used in our analysis can be viewed as exponential moving-average (EMA) estimates of past observations. This connects our theoretical quantities to EMA-based state tracking, which is widely used in deep learning optimization and training diagnostics Polyak and Juditsky (1992); Kingma and Ba (2014).

We make the following standard assumptions for the theoretical analysis. Specifically, Assumptions 2 and 1 are required for analyzing gradient descent, and Assumption 3 is required to ensure that the empirical loss and gradient estimators are unbiased.

Assumption 1 (Finite Optimization Domain).

There exists a closed convex 𝚯′\mathbf{\Theta}^{\prime} and D>0D>0 such that, for any θ,θ′\theta,\theta^{\prime} generated by the algorithm, there is θ,θ′∈𝚯′\theta,\theta^{\prime}\in\mathbf{\Theta}^{\prime} and ‖θ−θ′‖≤D\|\theta-\theta^{\prime}\|\leq D.

Assumption 2 (Bounded Lipschitz Loss).

There exists C,G>0C,G>0 such that, for all θ∈𝚯′\theta\in\mathbf{\Theta}^{\prime} and X∈𝕏X\in\mathbb{X}, ℓ⁡(θ,X)∈[0,C]\ell(\theta,X)\in[0,C] and ℓ\ell is GG-Lipschitz in θ\theta.

Assumption 3 (Source-Wise IID Sampling).

All data (i.e., prompts and responses, if applicable) collected by querying 𝒟k\mathcal{D}^{k} are sampled i.i.d. for all k∈[K]k\in[K].

We interpret the Lipschitz assumption as a regularity condition along the realized training trajectory rather than as a claim over the entire parameter space. Standard implementation techniques such as gradient clipping, KL regularization, and bounded reward design help control the observed loss variation as is illustrated in Appendix D.5, providing empirical evidence consistent with the assumptions. Furthermore, the low-epoch regime of LLM post-training ensures that most training samples are observed at most once, which is aligned with the source-wise i.i.d. assumption.

3 Method

3.1 DUCB-OGD: High-level Description

The training of modern deep neural networks, especially LLMs, relies heavily on well-optimized libraries. A standard pipeline typically involves a sampler, which selects a mini-batch of data samples as the model inputs, and an optimizer, which updates the model parameters using gradients computed from those mini-batches. Thus, we consider a two-player sampler-optimizer framework for seamless deployment in real-world training systems.

Optimizer. Recall that in each step tt, the sampler generates a mini-batch of training samples ℬt\mathcal{B}_{t} from 𝒟kt\mathcal{D}^{k_{t}}. The optimizer updates the model parameters according to

θt+1←θt−η∇μ^kt(θt;ℬt),\theta_{t+1}\leftarrow\theta_{t}-\eta\nabla\hat{\mu}^{k_{t}}(\theta_{t};\mathcal{B}_{t}), (6)

where η\eta is the learning rate and μ^kt​(θt,ℬt)\hat{\mu}^{k_{t}}(\theta_{t};\mathcal{B}_{t}) is the average empirical loss. When each data source corresponds to a distinct task or domain (e.g., verbal reasoning v.s., math reasoning), the loss function depends on the data source selected at the current step. Thus the optimizer is an instance of online gradient descent (OGD) Hazan (2016). We analyze unprojected OGD under Assumption 1, which explicitly requires the iterates to remain in the optimization domain.

Sampler. At the beginning of each step tt, the sampler observes the algorithm trajectory 𝒜t−1\mathcal{A}_{t-1} and the historical empirical losses {μ^kτ​(θτ,ℬτ),τ=1,…,t−1}\{\hat{\mu}^{k_{\tau}}(\theta_{\tau};\mathcal{B}_{\tau}),\tau=1,\dots,t-1\}. Selecting which data source to query is challenging for three reasons. First, empirical mini-batch losses are stochastic estimates of the corresponding source-wise expected losses. Second, the sampling environment is non-stationary because the source-wise losses change as the optimizer updates the model parameters. Third, the sampler faces an exploration-exploitation tradeoff: it must collect enough observations from all sources to estimate their losses accurately, while also allocating samples to sources that appear to be currently worst-performing.

However, unlike the adversarial bandit settings, where losses could change arbitrarily over time, the variation in source-wise losses between consecutive steps is controlled by the OGD learning rate η\eta in Eq. 6 together with the Lipschitz condition in Assumption 2. Thus, the sampling problem is naturally related to slowly-varying non-stationary bandits (Krishnamurthy and Gopalan, 2025). While the classical upper-confidence-bound (UCB) algorithm suits stationary environments, we use Discounted UCB (or DUCB) (Garivier and Moulines, 2011), a simple UCB variant with a discounting mechanism.

Specifically, let 𝟙​{⋅}\mathbbm{1}\{\cdot\} be the indicator function. For a discount factor β∈[0,1)\beta\in[0,1), define the EMA estimate of the empirical loss of source kk at step tt as

μ^tk:=1Ntk​(β)∑τ=1t𝟙{kτ=k}⋅βt−τμ^k(θτ;ℬτ),Ntk(β):=∑τ=1t𝟙{kτ=k}⋅βt−τ.\hat{\mu}_{t}^{k}:=\frac{1}{N_{t}^{k}(\beta)}\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\mathbbm{1}\left\{k_{\tau}=k\right\}\cdot\beta^{t-\tau}\hat{\mu}^{k}(\theta_{\tau};\mathcal{B}_{\tau}),\quad N_{t}^{k}(\beta):=\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\mathbbm{1}\left\{k_{\tau}=k\right\}\cdot\beta^{t-\tau}. (7)

Here, Ntk​(β)N_{t}^{k}(\beta) reflects the effective sample size of source kk. Let H⁡(β):=1/(1−β)H(\beta):=1/(1-\beta) for β∈[0,1)\beta\in[0,1) (known as the effective horizon of a discounted sequence) and set H⁡(1)=TH(1)=T for undiscounted case.

During the first KK steps, DUCB performs initial exploration by selecting each source once, i.e., kt=tk_{t}=t for t=1,…,Kt=1,\dots,K. Then for t≥K+1t\geq K+1, it selects the source ktk_{t} as

kt←arg⁡maxk⁡(μ^t−1k+rt−1k),rt−1k:=2​C​2​α​ln⁡H​(β)Nt−1k​(β),k_{t}\leftarrow\arg\max_{k}~\big(\hat{\mu}_{t-1}^{k}+r_{t-1}^{k}\big),\quad r_{t-1}^{k}:=2C\sqrt{\frac{2\alpha\ln H(\beta)}{N_{t-1}^{k}(\beta)}}, (8)

where α>0\alpha>0 is a constant controlling the aggressiveness of exploration and CC bounds the loss as in Assumption 2. Equivalently, this sampling rule can be represented as a categorical distribution kt∼Cat⁡(pt)k_{t}\sim\operatorname{Cat}(p_{t}) over [K][K], with probabilities pt,k=𝟙{k=kt}p_{t,k}=\mathbbm{1}\{k=k_{t}\} for each k∈[K]k\in[K]. We discuss the implementation details of DUCB using practical LLM post-training libraries in Appendix B.

Intuitively, the DUCB index simply couples the normalized EMA estimated empirical loss μ^tk\hat{\mu}_{t}^{k} with an optimistic confidence radius of O(Ntk(β)−1/2)O(N_{t}^{k}(\beta)^{-1/2}) for each k∈[K]k\in[K]. Due to the recursive identity of Ntk(β)=βNt−1k(β)+𝟙{kt=k}N_{t}^{k}(\beta)=\beta N_{t-1}^{k}(\beta)+\mathbbm{1}\{k_{t}=k\}, the effective sample size of each data source decays by a factor of β\beta whenever it is not selected at the current step. This naturally reflects a loss of confidence in μ^tk\hat{\mu}_{t}^{k} over time, as the current model parameter θt\theta_{t} drifts further away from the states in which the historical losses were observed.

3.2 Main Theoretical Results

Now we present the theoretical guarantees of DUCB-OGD. While the milestones of the proof are outlined below, we provide the complete version in Appendix C.

Theorem 2 (Dynamic Minimax Regret of DUCB-OGD).

Suppose μk\mu^{k} is convex in θ\theta for all kk. Then with η=K−1/4T−3/4\eta=K^{-{1/4}}T^{-{3/4}} in Eq. 6 and β=1−K−1/2T−1/2\beta=1-K^{-{1/2}}T^{-{1/2}} in Eq. 7, DUCB-OGD satisfies

𝔼⁡[Rρ,γ​(DUCB−OGDT)]≤O~​(K14​T34),\mathbb{E}\bigl[R^{\rho,\gamma}(\operatorname{DUCB-OGD}_{T})\bigr]\leq\tilde{O}\bigl(K^{\frac{1}{4}}T^{\frac{3}{4}}\bigr), (9)

for any ρ,γ∈[1−T−1,1]\rho,\gamma\in[1-T^{-1},1].

In other words, the dynamic minimax regret achieves the rate of O~​(K14​T34)\tilde{O}(K^{\frac{1}{4}}T^{\frac{3}{4}}) in both undiscounted (OPENρ=γ=1)\rho=\gamma=1) and discounted scheme (1−T−1≤ρ,γ<11-T^{-1}\leq\rho,\gamma<1). To prove this, we first present the OGD optimization regret and the DUCB bandit regret respectively, and then combine them to obtain the overall dynamic minimax regret.

Proposition 3 (Optimization Regret of OGD).

Suppose μk\mu^{k} is convex in θ\theta for all kk. OGD satisfies

TNT​(ρ)​𝔼​[Roρ​(OGDT)]≤O⁡(η−1)+O⁡(η​T),\frac{T}{N_{T}(\rho)}\mathbb{E}\bigl[R_{o}^{\rho}(\operatorname{OGD}_{T})\bigr]\leq O\bigl(\eta^{-1}\bigr)+O\bigl(\eta T\bigr), (10)

for any ρ∈[1−T−1,1]\rho\in[1-T^{-1},1].

Remark.

In the standard analysis of undiscounted and discounted OGD, the RHS of Eq. 10 can be minimized by choosing η=O(T−1/2)\eta=O(T^{-1/2}), which gives the rate of O⁡(T1/2)O(T^{1/2}).

The proof of Proposition 3 follows the standard OGD analysis for convex Lipschitz functions, with modifications to account for the stochasticity in the empirical loss observations. The full version is provided in Appendix C.2. Crucially, while η=O⁡(Tξ)\eta=O(T^{\xi}) for any ξ∈(−1,0)\xi\in(-1,0) in Eq. 10 yields an optimization regret sublinear in TT, we defer the choice of η\eta here since it dictates the rate that the sampling environment changes for DUCB, dramatically affecting its behavior. Instead, we first present the bandit regret with also an η\eta factor, then jointly tune η\eta to optimize both regrets.

Proposition 4 (Bandit Regret of DUCB).

Suppose η=O⁡(Tξ)\eta=O(T^{\xi}) for some ξ∈[−3/2,0)\xi\in[-3/2,0). Then with β=1−η2/3K−1/3\beta=1-\eta^{2/3}K^{-1/3}, DUCB satisfies

TNT​(γ)​𝔼​[Rbγ​(DUCBT)]≤O~​(η13​K13​T),\frac{T}{N_{T}(\gamma)}\mathbb{E}\bigl[R_{b}^{\gamma}(\operatorname{DUCB}_{T})\bigr]\leq\tilde{O}\bigl(\eta^{\frac{1}{3}}K^{\frac{1}{3}}T\bigr), (11)

for any γ∈[1−T−1,1]\gamma\in[1-T^{-1},1] and any KK independent of TT.

Remark.

Note that when γ=1\gamma=1, Rb1​(DUCB)R_{b}^{1}(\operatorname{DUCB}) matches the standard regret of slowly-varying non-stationary bandits by Krishnamurthy and Gopalan (2025). Alternatively, let V:=O⁡(η​T)V:=O(\eta T) be the total variation budget of the sampling environment over TT steps. Then Proposition 4 can be rewritten as Rb1​(DUCB)≤O~​(K13​T23​V13)R_{b}^{1}(\operatorname{DUCB})\leq\tilde{O}(K^{\frac{1}{3}}T^{\frac{2}{3}}V^{\frac{1}{3}}), matching the result of Besbes et al. (2014).

We provide a proof outline of Proposition 4. While standard DUCB analysis focuses on abruptly changing environments Garivier and Moulines (2011), we adapt the proof to our slowly-varying environment based on the following decomposition. Denote kt⋆:=arg​maxk⁡μk​(θt)k_{t}^{\star}:=\argmax_{k}\mu^{k}(\theta_{t}). Let μ~tk:=𝔼⁡[μ^tk|𝒜t]\tilde{\mu}_{t}^{k}:=\mathbb{E}[\hat{\mu}_{t}^{k}|\mathcal{A}_{t}] be the expected EMA estimated loss of the source kk at step tt. Then by Definition 2, we have Rbγ​(𝒜T)=∑t=1TγT−t​(μkt⋆​(θt)−μkt​(θt))R_{b}^{\gamma}(\mathcal{A}_{T})=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\gamma^{T-t}(\mu^{k_{t}^{\star}}(\theta_{t})-\mu^{k_{t}}(\theta_{t})), and for any t∈[T]t\in[T],

μkt⋆​(θt)−μkt​(θt)=(μ~t−1kt⋆−μ~t−1kt)⏟Term 1−(μ~t−1kt⋆−μkt⋆​(θt))⏟Term 2+(μ~t−1kt−μkt​(θt))⏟Term 3.\mu^{k_{t}^{\star}}(\theta_{t})-\mu^{k_{t}}(\theta_{t})=\underbrace{\bigl(\tilde{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}^{\star}}-\tilde{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}}\bigr)}_{\text{Term 1}}-\underbrace{\bigl(\tilde{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}^{\star}}-\mu^{k_{t}^{\star}}(\theta_{t})\bigr)}_{\text{Term 2}}+\underbrace{\bigl(\tilde{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}}-\mu^{k_{t}}(\theta_{t})\bigr)}_{\text{Term 3}}. (12)

We prove in Proposition 7 in Appendix C.4 that the DUCB update rule guarantees that Term 1 is bounded by O⁡(rt−1k)O(r_{t-1}^{k}) with high probability, where rt−1kr_{t-1}^{k} is the confidence radius defined in Eq. 8. Terms 2 and 3 reflect the bias of the EMA estimated loss w.r.t. the true loss, which are shown to be bounded by O~​(η​G2​H​(β))\tilde{O}(\eta G^{2}H(\beta)) in Proposition 8 in Appendix C.5. The complete proof of Proposition 4 is provided in Appendix C.3. Now we can prove Theorem 2.

Proof of Theorem 2.

Recall that the optimization regret in Proposition 3 is sublinear only when η=O⁡(Tξ)\eta=O(T^{\xi}) for some ξ∈(−1,0)\xi\in(-1,0), which satisfies the condition of Proposition 4. Then by Definition 3, and using Proposition 3 and Proposition 4, we have

𝔼⁡[Rρ,γ​(DUCB−OGDT)]≤O⁡(η−1)+O⁡(η​T)+O~​(η13​K13​T).\mathbb{E}\bigl[R^{\rho,\gamma}(\operatorname{DUCB-OGD}_{T})\bigr]\leq O\bigl(\eta^{-1}\bigr)+O\bigl(\eta T\bigr)+\tilde{O}\bigl(\eta^{\frac{1}{3}}K^{\frac{1}{3}}T\bigr). (13)

The RHS is minimized (order-wise) by taking η=K−1/4T−3/4\eta=K^{-{1/4}}T^{-{3/4}}, which concludes the proof. ∎

Further note that when ρ=γ\rho=\gamma, the average dynamic minimax regret Rρ,γ/TR^{\rho,\gamma}/T gives the minimax optimality gap measured by the EMA estimated worst-case loss. Then the following result is a direct consequence of Theorem 2.

Corollary 5.

Under the conditions of Theorem 2, the expected minimax optimality gap at the EMA-weighted iterate of DUCB−OGDT\operatorname{DUCB-OGD}_{T}, for any discount factor γ∈[1−T−1,1]\gamma\in[1-T^{-1},1], satisfies

𝔼⁡[maxk∈[K]⁡μk​(θ~Tγ)]−maxk∈[K]⁡μk​(θ⋆)≤O~​(K14​T−14),\mathbb{E}\left[\max_{k\in[K]}~\mu^{k}(\tilde{\theta}_{T}^{\gamma})\right]-\max_{k\in[K]}~\mu^{k}(\theta^{\star})\leq\tilde{O}\bigl(K^{\frac{1}{4}}T^{-\frac{1}{4}}\bigr), (14)

where θ~Tγ:=∑t=1TγT−t​θt/NT​(γ)\tilde{\theta}_{T}^{\gamma}:=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\gamma^{T-t}\theta_{t}/N_{T}(\gamma).

Specifically when ρ=γ=1\rho=\gamma=1, the results in Propositions 3 and 4 are shown to be optimal up to logarithmic factors. This follows from the lower bounds for the optimization regret and the dynamic bandit regret, by Hazan (2016) and Krishnamurthy and Gopalan (2025) respectively, based on constructing a hard instance where the loss landscape is non-smooth, and the worst-performing data source alters periodically over time. Then it immediately follows that, in the undiscounted setting, the bound in Theorem 2 is also optimal.

Theorem 6 (Lower Bound).

For every admissible sampler-optimizer algorithm 𝒜T\mathcal{A}_{T}, there exsits a problem instance for which the undiscounted regret satisfies 𝔼⁡[R1,1​(𝒜T)]≥Ω~​(K14​T34)\mathbb{E}[R^{1,1}(\mathcal{A}_{T})]\geq\tilde{\Omega}(K^{\frac{1}{4}}T^{\frac{3}{4}}).

3.3 Implications

We highlight two implications following the theoretical analysis.

Comparison to Pseudo-Regret GDRO. Other GDRO frameworks proposed by Zhang et al. (2023) and Soma et al. (2025) adopt the notion of pseudo regret, defined as R~​(𝒜T):=max⁡∑t=1Tk⁡μk​(θt)−T​maxk​μk​(θ⋆)\tilde{R}(\mathcal{A}_{T}):=\max_{k}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mu^{k}(\theta_{t})-T\max_{k}\mu^{k}(\theta^{\star}), which can be bounded by O~​(K1/2​T1/2)\tilde{O}(K^{1/2}T^{1/2}). The pseudo regret is fundamentally easier to analyze than our dynamic regret in Definition 1, since it always holds that R~≤R\tilde{R}\leq R (and R≤R1,1R\leq R^{1,1} by Proposition 1). In real-world learning problems such as LLM post-training, the worst-case data source may vary as the training progresses, and dynamic regret captures this by tracking the gap w.r.t. the worst-case loss in each step (we provide an example in Section 4.3). Moreover, pseudo regret controls only the uniform time-average of algorithm performance, while our dynamic-regret formulation yields guarantees for exponentially weighted trajectory averages emphasizing on later iterates as shown in Corollary 5. This better matches the practical deep learning workflows, where training dynamics are often monitored through EMA-style statistics and final checkpoints are selected from the later stage of model training.

Scope of the Lower Bound. We further note that Theorem 6 establishes optimality for the undiscounted objective under the instantaneous mini-batch-only feedback oracle, and does not imply optimality for discounted objectives or when richer feedback is available. Indeed, Zang et al. (2025) re-evaluate historically collected samples under the current model and obtain a dynamic-regret rate of O~​(K1/2​T1/2)\tilde{O}(K^{1/2}T^{1/2}). Yet this stronger oracle requires expensive model evaluations over a linearly growing replay-buffer, and a generalization step from replay-based empirical losses to population losses.

4 Experiments

4.1 Objectives and Datasets

We evaluate DUCB-OGD across three LLM post-training objectives:

  • •

    SFT: We train base models for 32k samples on the Math and Orca sources of Tulu-v2 (Ivison et al., 2023) using TRL (von Werra et al., 2020). We evaluate the minimum of GSM8k accuracy (Cobbe et al., 2021) and IFEval prompt accuracy (Zhou et al., 2023).

  • •

    DPO: We train instruction-tuned models for 16k samples on the Code, Multilingual, and Stem sources of HelpSteer3 (Wang et al., 2025c; Wang et al., 2025e; Wang et al., 2025d) using TRL. The primary metric is minimum source-wise test preference accuracy.

  • •

    GRPO: We consider (i) Reasoning, comprising Arc, Countdown, and Zebra as three sources (Chollet, 2019; Katz et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2025), with a 10k-sample budget using Verl (Sheng et al., 2024); and (ii) CommonsenseQA (Talmor et al., 2019), partitioned into Social, Physical, Causal-Temporal, and General sources, with a 6.4k-sample budget using TRL. We report the minimum source-wise test accuracy.

For each objective, we train models of different sizes from the Qwen2.5 (Yang et al., 2024; Team, 2024), Qwen3 (Team, 2025), Llama3 (AI@Meta, 2024), and GLM4 (GLM et al., 2024) families using different sampling algorithms.

4.2 Robustness Across Post-Training Objectives and Model Families

Table 2 reports minimum source-wise accuracy as the primary metric and unweighted average accuracy as a reference. All metrics are evaluated at the final training checkpoint. Additional models and metrics are reported in Appendix D.

For SFT, we evaluate an adapted Exp3-style proxy based on DynamixSFT (Shin et al., 2025). A faithful implementation requires virtual parameter updates to estimate anticipated source-wise loss decreases and is not directly compatible with our training pipeline, and our proxy instead uses observed source-wise loss decreases. DUCB achieves the highest minimum accuracy for both models, whereas the Exp3-style sampler obtains higher average accuracy, illustrating the robustness-average performance trade-off.

For DPO, we compare against faithful implementations of AutoMixAlign Corrado et al. (2025), including both AMA-R and AMA-S. AutoMixAlign uses source-specific specialist models to compute excess-loss-based sampling signals, which requires training KK additional specialists before the generalist model. DUCB achieves competitive or better worst-source performance without this auxiliary training cost. These results further support the robustness of DUCB under a substantially lighter feedback and computational requirement. Specifically, across three Qwen2.5-3B runs, DUCB obtains 79.33±0.6279.33\pm 0.62 minimum accuracy versus 76.76±1.6576.76\pm 1.65 for Uniform, corresponding to a paired gain of 2.57±1.042.57\pm 1.04 percentage points.

For GRPO, we compare against an Exp3-style sampler-only proxy of MT-GRPO Ramesh et al. (2026) and a faithful implementation of DUMP Wang et al. (2025b) which adopts a switching-window UCB sampler. We use the source-wise training reward with improvement correction and the training advantage as the sampling signal, respectively. We omit additional components of MT-GRPO such as rollout filtering and only implement the sampler in order to maintain uniformity with other samplers and compatibility between the TRL and Verl libraries. The results show clear margins of DUCB over other uniform and adaptive sampling baselines on the minimum accuracies across both datasets.

Across the six main settings, DUCB achieves the highest minimum accuracy in five and remains competitive with AMA-S in the remaining DPO setting. Detailed discussions of the results are also provided in Appendix D.

4.3 Computation Efficiency and Dynamic Worst-Source Adaptation

We specifically discuss the following two aspects of the proposed DUCB-OGD algorithm compared with other evaluated baselines.

Training Overhead.

We measure per-step runtime across three Qwen2.5-3B DPO runs, with full results reported in Appendix D.4. DUCB requires 21.94±1.1421.94\pm 1.14 seconds per step, compared with 21.90±1.2921.90\pm 1.29 for Uniform; the difference is small relative to the observed run-to-run variation. Its sampler adds no auxiliary model evaluations and maintains only O⁡(K)O(K) scalar state. By comparison, AMA additionally trains KK source-specific specialists before training the generalist model. Thus, DUCB introduces little measurable online overhead beyond the underlying LLM training step and avoids AMA’s auxiliary specialist-training cost.

Adaptation to Evolving Source Difficulty.

We further compare DUCB’s instantaneous tracking with the cumulative-reward updates of Exp3 on the Arc and Countdown sources of the Reasoning task in Fig. 1. Arc initially has higher reward than Countdown, but this ordering later reverses, making Arc the new worst-performing source. DUCB shifts its sampling priority toward Arc shortly after the crossover, whereas Exp3 continues to favor Countdown until later observations outweigh its accumulated history. This representative example, together with the switching frequencies in Tab. 1, illustrates DUCB’s ability to adapt to changing source difficulty. Because instantaneous tracking is also more sensitive to short-term reward variation, we use DEMA smoothing and forced exploration as practical stabilizers, detailed in Appendix B.

5 Conclusion

We study dynamic minimax regret for robust multi-source LLM post-training under instantaneous mini-batch-only bandit feedback. We propose DUCB-OGD, which couples discounted UCB sampling with online gradient descent and requires neither historical re-evaluation nor auxiliary model evaluations. Across SFT, DPO, and GRPO, DUCB-OGD achieves the highest minimum source-wise accuracy in the majority of the settings and remains competitive with contemporary baselines but avoids expensive model re-evaluations. Frequent worst-source switching is observed across all three objectives, while DUCB’s per-step runtime remains close to Uniform, supporting the relevance and practical efficiency of instantaneous dynamic tracking.

It is shown that DUCB-OGD is most applicable when worst-source robustness is the primary objective, source difficulty changes during training, and only instantaneous mini-batch feedback is available or affordable due to practical constraints. Trade-offs may occur between worst-source and average performances. The guarantees involving optimization also do not cover non-convex loss landscapes. Our comparisons include both faithful baseline implementations and explicitly adapted sampler-only proxies, which avoid objective-specific training modifications. The evaluation is limited to 0.5B-9B models and unimodal datasets with relatively few sources. The performance on larger models and datasets with more complicated distributional characteristics remains to be studied.

AI Use Statement

In this work, we did not use generative AI tools to generate datasets, develop theoretical models or methods, formulate or prove mathematical claims, design experiments, implement methods, process data, or interpret experimental results. We used generative AI tools only to polish writing and improve readability. We reviewed the accuracy and consistency of all AI-assisted work, including revised text, equations, and descriptions of experimental results. We take responsibility for the final content of this work, including all text, claims, and artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.

Reproducibility statement

We provide the complete DUCB-OGD algorithm and theoretical assumptions in the main text, with full proofs in Appendix C. Appendix B and D document the implementation, practical stabilizers, key training configurations, and hyperparameters. The datasets, pretrained models, sample budgets, evaluation metrics, final-checkpoint protocol, multi-seed results, and hardware used for runtime measurements are described in Section 4 and Appendix D. All datasets and model checkpoints are publicly available and cited. We intend to release the training and evaluation code, full configurations, and scripts upon publication.
