Appendix

Appendix A Related Work

Distributionally Robust Optimization.

Distributionally Robust Optimization studies learning algorithms that optimize model performance under worst-case shifts or uncertainty in the data distribution Hu et al. (2018); Duchi and Namkoong (2021); Jin et al. (2021); Agarwal and Zhang (2022). Based on this formulation, GDRO explicitly minimizes the worst-case loss across predefined distribution groups Sagawa* et al. (2020); Haghtalab et al. (2022); Ghosal and Li (2023); Zhang et al. (2023). Recent theoretical work formulates GDRO as a stochastic convex-concave saddle-point problem and studies algorithms that combine data sampling with parameter optimization. For example, Zhang et al. (2023) use Exp3-style sampling  Auer et al. (2002a) to track the fixed worst-performing data source in hindsight, and bound the minimax optimality gap for the time-averaged model parameters, but does not account for the evolving nature of the training process. Closest to our setting, Zang et al. (2025) propose to track the adaptive sequence of worst-performing data sources using UCB-style sampling Auer et al. (2002a). However, their approach requires repeatedly re-evaluating the current model on previously collected samples to maintain up-to-date source-wise loss estimates. This introduces substantial computational overhead and requires intrusive modifications to the standard training pipeline, limiting its practibility and compatibility with modern LLM training libraries.

Non-stationary Bandits.

Multi-armed bandit algorithms provide a natural framework for adaptive data-source selection. Classical stochastic bandits assume fixed reward distributions Auer et al. (2002a), while adversarial bandits allow arbitrary reward sequences Auer et al. (2002b). Non-stationary bandits interpolate between these extremes by imposing structure on how rewards evolve over time Garivier and Moulines (2011); Besbes et al. (2014); Krishnamurthy and Gopalan (2025). Discounted-UCB methods were originally designed for environments with abrupt changes Garivier and Moulines (2011), while variation-budget and slowly-varying models provide alternative ways to quantify non-stationarity Besbes et al. (2014); Krishnamurthy and Gopalan (2025). Our setting differs from standard non-stationary bandits because the non-stationarity is endogenous: source-wise losses change because the optimizer updates the model parameters. Thus, the sampler and optimizer are coupled. We exploit this structure by combining discounted bandit estimation with online gradient descent and analyzing the resulting sampler-optimizer behavior through dynamic minimax regret.

Adaptive Sampling for LLM Training.

Adaptive sampling has become increasingly important in LLM training and post-training because data sources vary widely in quality, difficulty, and relevance. Some methods estimate mixture weights offline using data-value models, filtering scores, or proxy evaluations Lin et al. (2024); Lv et al. (2025); Wang et al. (2025a); Sachdeva et al. (2026). Others update sampling probabilities online using training losses, gradient statistics, task difficulty, or model feedback Shin et al. (2025); Koh et al. (2026); Chen et al. (2025); Wang et al. (2025b); Sun et al. (2026); Panaganti et al. (2026). Recent work on multi-task post-training also studies how to balance heterogeneous reasoning, coding, safety, and instruction-following data so that easier or larger sources do not dominate the training Li et al. (2026); Ramesh et al. (2026); Wu et al. (2026); Panaganti et al. (2026). DRO-inspired objectives have also been explored for improving worst-case performance across groups or domains Oren et al. (2019); Corrado et al. (2025); Wang et al. (2026); Shao et al. (2026). However, existing approaches typically optimize static or heuristic objectives and lack a principled dynamic minimax regret formulation that explicitly accounts for the non-stationary nature of LLM training while providing provable theoretical guarantees.

Appendix B Implementation Details

The training process is outlined in Algorithm 1. We further adopt the following techniques during implementation.

Batch Sampling.

Instead of selecting only one data source in each step, we propose a sampling version of DUCB, defined as

kt←arg​maxk∈[K]⁡μ^t−1k+ϕt−1k,ϕt−1k∼𝒩⁡(2​rt−1k,C22​Nt−1k​(β)).k_{t}\leftarrow\argmax_{k\in[K]}~\hat{\mu}_{t-1}^{k}+\phi_{t-1}^{k},\quad\phi_{t-1}^{k}\sim\mathcal{N}\Bigg(2r_{t-1}^{k},\frac{C^{2}}{2N_{t-1}^{k}(\beta)}\Bigg).

Due to the stochasticity of ϕt−1k\phi_{t-1}^{k}, the selection rule induces a non-degenerate categorical distribution over [K][K] with probabilities ptp_{t} s.t. kt∼Cat⁡(pt)k_{t}\sim\operatorname{Cat}(p_{t}), as opposed to the deterministic rule in Eq. 8. Therefore, every mini-batch may contain a mixture of samples from multiple data sources shown by Algorithm 1. This is especially important when using a large batch size, since training on a large amount of samples from a single data source increases the risk of catastrophic forgetting or mode collapse. We further prove in Appendix C.6 that the bandit regret of the sampling version of DUCB is only a constant factor worse than that of the standard DUCB in Proposition 4. Since ptp_{t} does not admit a closed-form expression, we approximate it using the Gauss-Hermite quadrature (Butler and Moffitt, 1982). At the end of each training step, we update μ^tk\hat{\mu}_{t}^{k} and Ntk​(β)N_{t}^{k}(\beta) using the empirical loss and sample proportion in the mini-batch for each data source.

Double-EMA.

Traditional EMA is known to have a delayed response to changing inputs due to the discounting mechanism. Thus we employ double-EMA Mulloy (1994) to track the training losses in the implementation of all samplers, defined as

DoubleEma​(x)←2⋅Ema​(x)−Ema​(Ema​(x)).\textsc{DoubleEma}(x)\leftarrow 2\cdot\textsc{Ema}(x)-\textsc{Ema}(\textsc{Ema}(x)).

As shown in Fig. 1, the DEMA reward is able to closely track the trend of raw reward while providing sufficient denoising ability.

Enforced Exploration.

In the early stage of training, the sampling weights of DUCB can be affected by noisy initial observations and experience fluctuations. Inspired by Exp3 (and its variants), we augment the sampling weights by

ptk←(1−βt)​ptk+βtK,∀k∈[K].p_{t}^{k}\leftarrow(1-\beta^{t})p_{t}^{k}+\frac{\beta^{t}}{K},\quad\forall k\in[K].

This enforces uniform exploration across all data sources in the early stage of training, and exponentially decays as the training progresses and becomes more stable. It is worth noting that the extra regret incurred by the enforced exploration is at most O⁡(H⁡(β))O(H(\beta)), which is dominated by the standard DUCB regret given the choice of β\beta in Proposition 4.

Appendix C Proofs

C.1 Proof of Proposition 1

Proof of Proposition 1.

Recall that kt⋆=maxk⁡μk​(θ)k_{t}^{\star}=\max_{k}\mu^{k}(\theta). By Definition 2,

Ro1​(𝒜T)+Rb1​(𝒜T)=∑t=1T(μkt​(θt)−μkt​(θ⋆))+∑t=1T(μkt⋆​(θt)−μkt​(θt))=∑t=1T(μkt⋆​(θt)−μkt​(θ⋆))≥∑t=1Tμkt⋆​(θt)−T​maxk∈[K]​μk​(θ⋆),\begin{aligned} R_{o}^{1}(\mathcal{A}_{T})+R_{b}^{1}(\mathcal{A}_{T})&=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\Big(\mu^{k_{t}}(\theta_{t})-\mu^{k_{t}}(\theta^{\star})\Big)+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\Big(\mu^{k_{t}^{\star}}(\theta_{t})-\mu^{k_{t}}(\theta_{t})\Big)\\ &=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\Big(\mu^{k_{t}^{\star}}(\theta_{t})-\mu^{k_{t}}(\theta^{\star})\Big)\\ &\geq\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mu^{k_{t}^{\star}}(\theta_{t})-T\max_{k\in[K]}~\mu^{k}(\theta^{\star})\\ \end{aligned},

where the last inequality follows from the fact that maxk⁡μk​(θ)≥μkt​(θ)\max_{k}\mu^{k}(\theta)\geq\mu^{k_{t}}(\theta) for all θ\theta and tt. Further recalling Definition 1 concludes the proof. ∎

C.2 Proof of Proposition 3

The proof follows from standard results for undiscounted and discounted OGD. Suppose a player of an online game observes a sequence of losses {ft​(θt),t=1,…,T}\{f_{t}(\theta_{t}),t=1,\dots,T\} for TT steps, and updates the parameter using OGD defined in Eq. 6. Then the following lemmas hold. Note that we defer the choice of η\eta in both cases.

Lemma 1 (Undiscounted OGD (Hazan, 2016)).

For any θ∈𝚯\theta\in\mathbf{\Theta}, OGD satisfies

∑t=1Tft​(θt)−∑t=1Tft​(θ)≤D2η+η​G2​T.\sum_{t=1}^{T}f_{t}(\theta_{t})-\sum_{t=1}^{T}f_{t}(\theta)\leq\frac{D^{2}}{\eta}+\eta G^{2}T.
Lemma 2 (Discounted OGD (Yang et al., 2026)).

Let ρ∈[0,1)\rho\in[0,1) be a discount factor. For any θ∈𝚯\theta\in\mathbf{\Theta}, OGD satisfies

∑t=1TρT−t​ft​(θt)−∑t=1TρT−t​ft​(θ)≤((1−ρ)​D2η+η​G22)​NT​(ρ).\sum_{t=1}^{T}\rho^{T-t}f_{t}(\theta_{t})-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\rho^{T-t}f_{t}(\theta)\leq\Biggl(\frac{(1-\rho)D^{2}}{\eta}+\frac{\eta G^{2}}{2}\Biggr)N_{T}(\rho).

Now we can prove the optimization regret.

Proof of Proposition 3.

Let ft​(θt)=μ^kt​(θt,ℬt)f_{t}(\theta_{t})=\hat{\mu}^{k_{t}}(\theta_{t};\mathcal{B}_{t}). Recall that X∼𝒟ktX\sim\mathcal{D}^{k_{t}} i.i.d. for all X∈ℬtX\in\mathcal{B}_{t} according to Assumption 3, i.e.,

𝔼[μ^kt(θt;ℬt)|kt,θt]=μkt(θt).\mathbb{E}\bigl[\hat{\mu}^{k_{t}}(\theta_{t};\mathcal{B}_{t})\big|k_{t},\theta_{t}\bigr]=\mu^{k_{t}}(\theta_{t}).

Since θ⋆∈𝚯\theta^{\star}\in\mathbf{\Theta} is fixed, we have, by Lemma 1,

𝔼⁡[Ro1​(𝒜T)]=∑t=1T𝔼⁡[μkt​(θt)−μkt​(θ⋆)]=∑t=1T𝔼[𝔼[μ^kt(θt;ℬt)−μ^kt(θ⋆;ℬt)|kt,θt]]=𝔼⁡[∑t=1Tμ^kt​(θt,ℬt)−∑t=1Tμ^kt​(θ⋆,ℬt)]≤D2η+η​G2​T,\begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}\bigl[R_{o}^{1}(\mathcal{A}_{T})\bigr]&=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mu^{k_{t}}(\theta_{t})-\mu^{k_{t}}(\theta^{\star})\bigr]\\ &=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathbb{E}\bigl[\hat{\mu}^{k_{t}}(\theta_{t};\mathcal{B}_{t})-\hat{\mu}^{k_{t}}(\theta^{\star};\mathcal{B}_{t})\big|k_{t},\theta_{t}\bigr]\bigr]\\ &=\mathbb{E}\Biggl[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\hat{\mu}^{k_{t}}(\theta_{t};\mathcal{B}_{t})-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\hat{\mu}^{k_{t}}(\theta^{\star};\mathcal{B}_{t})\Biggr]\\ &\leq\frac{D^{2}}{\eta}+\eta G^{2}T\end{aligned},

and similarly by Lemma 2,

𝔼⁡[Roρ​(𝒜T)]≤((1−ρ)​D2η+η​G22)​NT​(ρ),∀ρ∈[0,1).\mathbb{E}\bigl[R_{o}^{\rho}(\mathcal{A}_{T})\bigr]\leq\Biggl(\frac{(1-\rho)D^{2}}{\eta}+\frac{\eta G^{2}}{2}\Biggr)N_{T}(\rho),\quad\forall\rho\in[0,1).

Further note that NT​(1)=TN_{T}(1)=T. Combining together, we have

TNT​(ρ)​𝔼​[Roρ​(𝒜T)]≤O⁡(η−1​(1−ρ)​T)+O⁡(η​T)≤O⁡(η−1)+O⁡(η​T),\frac{T}{N_{T}(\rho)}\mathbb{E}\bigl[R_{o}^{\rho}(\mathcal{A}_{T})\bigr]\leq O\bigl(\eta^{-1}(1-\rho)T\bigr)+O\bigl(\eta T\bigr)\leq O\bigl(\eta^{-1}\bigr)+O\bigl(\eta T\bigr),

for any ρ∈[1−T−1,1]\rho\in[1-T^{-1},1], which concludes the proof. ∎

C.3 Proof of Proposition 4

We first present the following results, proved respectively in Sections C.4 and C.5. As opposed to stationary bandits, the explorations for non-stationary bandits conducted in distant steps gradually expire due to changing environments. Therefore, continuous re-exploration is needed to ensure reliable concentration results, i.e., we need to keep Ntk​(β)N_{t}^{k}(\beta) above some threshold A>0A>0.

Proposition 7 (Bandit Gap of DUCB).

Suppose DUCB picks ktk_{t} in step t≥K+1t\geq K+1 as in Eq. 8. Then for any A>0A>0,

Pr[μ~t−1kt⋆−μ~t−1kt>2rtkt1+A−1,Nt−1kt(β)≥A]≤2H(β)−α.\Pr\left[\tilde{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}^{\star}}-\tilde{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}}>2r_{t}^{k_{t}}\sqrt{1+A^{-1}},N_{t-1}^{k_{t}}(\beta)\geq A\right]\leq 2H(\beta)^{-\alpha}.
Proposition 8 (EMA Bias).

Suppose {θt,t=1,…,T}\{\theta_{t},t=1,\dots,T\} is generated by OGD with learning rate η\eta as in Eq. 6. Then for any t∈[T]t\in[T] and A>0A>0 s.t. Ntk​(β)≥AN_{t}^{k}(\beta)\geq A,

|μ~tk−μk​(θt+1)|≤η​G2​H​(β)​ln⁡(2​C​eη​A​G2),\left|\tilde{\mu}_{t}^{k}-\mu^{k}(\theta_{t+1})\right|\leq\eta G^{2}H(\beta)\ln\left(\frac{2Ce}{\eta AG^{2}}\right),

where β≥1/2\beta\geq 1/2 and H⁡(β)H(\beta) is the effective horizon as in Eq. 8.

We further state following lemmas.

Lemma 3.

For any τ∈[T]\tau\in[T] and constant A>0A>0,

∑t=K+1T𝟙​{kt=k,Nt−1k​(β)<A}⋅γT−t≤⌈T/τ⌉​Nβ−τ​Ak​(γ).\sum_{t=K+1}^{T}\mathbbm{1}\left\{k_{t}=k,N_{t-1}^{k}(\beta)<A\right\}\cdot\gamma^{T-t}\leq\lceil T/\tau\rceil N_{\beta^{-\tau}A}^{k}(\gamma).
Proof.

We first write

∑t=K+1T𝟙​{kt=k,Nt−1k​(β)<A}⋅γT−t≤∑m=1⌈T/τ⌉∑t=(m−1)​τm​τ𝟙​{kt=k,Nt−1k​(β)<A}⋅γT−t.\sum_{t=K+1}^{T}\mathbbm{1}\left\{k_{t}=k,N_{t-1}^{k}(\beta)<A\right\}\cdot\gamma^{T-t}\leq\sum_{m=1}^{\lceil{T/\tau}\rceil}\sum_{t=(m-1)\tau}^{m\tau}\mathbbm{1}\left\{k_{t}=k,N_{t-1}^{k}(\beta)<A\right\}\cdot\gamma^{T-t}.

By Garivier and Moulines (2011) (Lemma 25 and Corollary 26),

∑t=(m−1)​τm​τ𝟙​{kt=k,Nt−1k​(β)<A}≤β−τ​A.\sum_{t=(m-1)\tau}^{m\tau}\mathbbm{1}\left\{k_{t}=k,N_{t-1}^{k}(\beta)<A\right\}\leq\beta^{-\tau}A.

Further note that

∑t=(m−1)​τm​τ𝟙​{kt=k,Nt−1k​(β)<A}⋅γT−t=γT−m​τ​∑t=(m−1)​τm​τ𝟙​{kt=k,Nt−1k​(β)<A}⋅γm​τ−t≤γT−m​τ​Nβ−τ​Ak​(γ)≤Nβ−τ​Ak​(γ).\begin{aligned} \sum_{t=(m-1)\tau}^{m\tau}&\mathbbm{1}\left\{k_{t}=k,N_{t-1}^{k}(\beta)<A\right\}\cdot\gamma^{T-t}\\ &=\gamma^{T-m\tau}\sum_{t=(m-1)\tau}^{m\tau}\mathbbm{1}\left\{k_{t}=k,N_{t-1}^{k}(\beta)<A\right\}\cdot\gamma^{m\tau-t}\\ &\leq\gamma^{T-m\tau}N_{\beta^{-\tau}A}^{k}(\gamma)\\ &\leq N_{\beta^{-\tau}A}^{k}(\gamma)\\ \end{aligned}.

Plugging back to the first equation concludes the proof. ∎

Lemma 4.

For all T≥K+1T\geq K+1,

∑t=K+1T𝟙{kt=k}⋅γT−tNtk​(β)≤2​NTk​(β)12+NTk​(γ)​H​(β)−12.\sum_{t=K+1}^{T}\frac{\mathbbm{1}\left\{k_{t}=k\right\}\cdot\gamma^{T-t}}{\sqrt{N_{t}^{k}(\beta)}}\leq 2N_{T}^{k}(\beta)^{\frac{1}{2}}+N_{T}^{k}(\gamma)H(\beta)^{-\frac{1}{2}}.
Proof.

Recall that

𝟙{kt=k}=Ntk(β)−βNt−1k(β)=Ntk(β)−Nt−1k(β)+(1−β)Nt−1k(β).\mathbbm{1}\{k_{t}=k\}=N_{t}^{k}(\beta)-\beta N_{t-1}^{k}(\beta)=N_{t}^{k}(\beta)-N_{t-1}^{k}(\beta)+(1-\beta)N_{t-1}^{k}(\beta).

Thus we can write

𝟙{kt=k}Ntk​(β)=𝟙{kt=k}2Ntk​(β)=𝟙{kt=k}⋅Ntk​(β)−Nt−1k​(β)Ntk​(β)+𝟙{kt=k}⋅(1−β)​Nt−1k​(β)Ntk​(β).\begin{aligned} \frac{\mathbbm{1}\left\{k_{t}=k\right\}}{\sqrt{N_{t}^{k}(\beta)}}&=\frac{\mathbbm{1}\left\{k_{t}=k\right\}^{2}}{\sqrt{N_{t}^{k}(\beta)}}\\ &=\mathbbm{1}\left\{k_{t}=k\right\}\cdot\frac{N_{t}^{k}(\beta)-N_{t-1}^{k}(\beta)}{\sqrt{N_{t}^{k}(\beta)}}+\mathbbm{1}\left\{k_{t}=k\right\}\cdot\frac{(1-\beta)N_{t-1}^{k}(\beta)}{\sqrt{N_{t}^{k}(\beta)}}\end{aligned}.

For the first term, note that

Ntk​(β)−Nt−1k​(β)Ntk​(β)≤2​(Ntk​(β)−Nt−1k​(β)).\frac{N_{t}^{k}(\beta)-N_{t-1}^{k}(\beta)}{\sqrt{N_{t}^{k}(\beta)}}\leq 2\Bigl(\sqrt{N_{t}^{k}(\beta)}-\sqrt{N_{t-1}^{k}(\beta)}\Bigr).

Since γ≤1\gamma\leq 1 and Ntk​(β)≥Nt−1k​(β)N_{t}^{k}(\beta)\geq N_{t-1}^{k}(\beta) whenever kt=kk_{t}=k, we have

∑t=K+1T𝟙{kt=k}⋅γT−t(Ntk​(β)−Nt−1k​(β)Ntk​(β))≤∑t=K+1T(Ntk​(β)−Nt−1k​(β)Ntk​(β))≤2​∑t=K+1T(Ntk​(β)−Nt−1k​(β))≤2​NTk​(β)12.\begin{aligned} \sum_{t=K+1}^{T}\mathbbm{1}\left\{k_{t}=k\right\}\cdot\gamma^{T-t}\Biggl(\frac{N_{t}^{k}(\beta)-N_{t-1}^{k}(\beta)}{\sqrt{N_{t}^{k}(\beta)}}\Biggr)&\leq\sum_{t=K+1}^{T}\Biggl(\frac{N_{t}^{k}(\beta)-N_{t-1}^{k}(\beta)}{\sqrt{N_{t}^{k}(\beta)}}\Biggr)\\ &\leq 2\sum_{t=K+1}^{T}\Bigl(\sqrt{N_{t}^{k}(\beta)}-\sqrt{N_{t-1}^{k}(\beta)}\Bigr)\\ &\leq 2N_{T}^{k}(\beta)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\ \end{aligned}.

For the second term, note that Ntk​(β)≤H⁡(β)=1/(1−β)N_{t}^{k}(\beta)\leq H(\beta)=1/(1-\beta) for all tt. Thus

∑t=K+1T𝟙{kt=k}⋅γT−t((1−β)​Nt−1k​(β)Ntk​(β))≤(1−β)​∑t=K+1TγT−t​Nt−1k​(β)≤(1−β)​NTk​(β)12​∑t=K+1TγT−t≤NTk​(γ)​H​(β)−12.\begin{aligned} \sum_{t=K+1}^{T}\mathbbm{1}\left\{k_{t}=k\right\}\cdot\gamma^{T-t}\Bigg(\frac{(1-\beta)N_{t-1}^{k}(\beta)}{\sqrt{N_{t}^{k}(\beta)}}\Biggr)&\leq(1-\beta)\sum_{t=K+1}^{T}\gamma^{T-t}\sqrt{N_{t-1}^{k}(\beta)}\\ &\leq(1-\beta)N_{T}^{k}(\beta)^{\frac{1}{2}}\sum_{t=K+1}^{T}\gamma^{T-t}\\ &\leq N_{T}^{k}(\gamma)H(\beta)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\\ \end{aligned}.

Combining together gives the statement of the lemma. ∎

Now we can prove the dynamic bandit regret. In fact, we prove a more explicit version as follows.

Proposition 9 (Unnormalized Dynamic Bandit Regret of DUCB).

For any β≥1/2\beta\geq 1/2, DUCB satisfies

𝔼⁡[Rbγ​(DUCBT)]≤\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigl[R_{b}^{\gamma}(\operatorname{DUCB}_{T})\bigr]\leq O⁡(K​T​H​(β)−1)+O~​(K12​H​(β)12)\displaystyle O\bigl(KTH(\beta)^{-1}\bigr)+\tilde{O}\bigl(K^{\frac{1}{2}}H(\beta)^{\frac{1}{2}}\bigr)
+O~​(NT​(γ)​H​(β)−12)+O~​(η​NT​(γ)​H​(β)).\displaystyle+\tilde{O}\bigl(N_{T}(\gamma)H(\beta)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\bigr)+\tilde{O}\bigl(\eta N_{T}(\gamma)H(\beta)\bigr).
Proof.

Let A≥1/3A\geq 1/3 be a constant. We start by writing

Rbγ​(DUCBT)=∑t=1TγT−t​(μkt⋆​(θt)−μkt​(θt))≤γT−KKC+C∑t=K+1T𝟙{Nt−1kt(β)<A}⋅γT−t+∑t=K+1T𝟙{Nt−1kt(β)≥A}⋅γT−t(μkt⋆(θt)−μkt(θt)).\begin{aligned} R_{b}^{\gamma}(\operatorname{DUCB}_{T})=&~\sum_{t=1}^{T}\gamma^{T-t}\Bigl(\mu^{k_{t}^{\star}}(\theta_{t})-\mu^{k_{t}}(\theta_{t})\Bigr)\\ \leq&~\gamma^{T-K}KC+C\sum_{t=K+1}^{T}\mathbbm{1}\left\{N_{t-1}^{k_{t}}(\beta)<A\right\}\cdot\gamma^{T-t}\\ &~+\sum_{t=K+1}^{T}\mathbbm{1}\left\{N_{t-1}^{k_{t}}(\beta)\geq A\right\}\cdot\gamma^{T-t}\Bigl(\mu^{k_{t}^{\star}}(\theta_{t})-\mu^{k_{t}}(\theta_{t})\Bigr)\\ \end{aligned}.

Denote NT​(⋅)=∑k=1KNtk​(⋅)N_{T}(\cdot)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}N_{t}^{k}(\cdot). By Lemma 3, the first sum writes

C∑t=K+1T𝟙{Nt−1kt(β)<A}⋅γT−t≤C​∑k=1K∑t=K+1T𝟙​{kt=k,Nt−1k​(β)<A}⋅γT−t≤C​K​⌈T/τ⌉​Nβ−τ​A​(γ).\begin{aligned} C\sum_{t=K+1}^{T}\mathbbm{1}\left\{N_{t-1}^{k_{t}}(\beta)<A\right\}\cdot\gamma^{T-t}&\leq C\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{t=K+1}^{T}\mathbbm{1}\left\{k_{t}=k,N_{t-1}^{k}(\beta)<A\right\}\cdot\gamma^{T-t}\\ &\leq CK\lceil T/\tau\rceil N_{\beta^{-\tau}A}(\gamma)\\ \end{aligned}.

Letting τ=NT​(β)\tau=N_{T}(\beta), we have

β−τ=β−NT​(β)≤{β−1/(1−β)≤412≤β<11β=1.\beta^{-\tau}=\beta^{-N_{T}(\beta)}\leq\begin{cases}\begin{aligned} &\beta^{-1/(1-\beta)}\leq 4&\quad\frac{1}{2}\leq\beta<1\\ &1&\quad\beta=1\\ \end{aligned}\end{cases}.

Thus Nβ−τ​A​(γ)≤β−τ​A≤4​AN_{\beta^{-\tau}A}(\gamma)\leq\beta^{-\tau}A\leq 4A for all 1/2≤β≤11/2\leq\beta\leq 1, and

C∑t=K+1T𝟙{Nt−1kt(β)<A(β)}⋅γT−t≤4ACK(TNT(β)−1+1).C\sum_{t=K+1}^{T}\mathbbm{1}\left\{N_{t-1}^{k_{t}}(\beta)<A(\beta)\right\}\cdot\gamma^{T-t}\leq 4ACK\bigl(TN_{T}(\beta)^{-1}+1\bigr).

For the second sum, recall by Eq. 12 that

∑t=1TγT−t​(μkt⋆​(θt)CLOSEOPEN−μkt​(θt))=∑t=1TγT−t​(μ~t−1kt⋆−μ~t−1kt)+∑t=1TγT−t(μkt⋆(θt)−μ~t−1kt⋆)−∑t=1TγT−t(μkt(θt)−μ~t−1kt).\begin{aligned} \sum_{t=1}^{T}\gamma^{T-t}\bigl(\mu^{k_{t}^{\star}}(\theta_{t})&-\mu^{k_{t}}(\theta_{t})\bigr)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\gamma^{T-t}\bigl(\tilde{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}^{\star}}-\tilde{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}}\bigr)\\ &~+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\gamma^{T-t}\bigl(\mu^{k_{t}^{\star}}(\theta_{t})-\tilde{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}^{\star}}\bigr)-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\gamma^{T-t}\bigl(\mu^{k_{t}}(\theta_{t})-\tilde{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}}\bigr)\end{aligned}.

By Proposition 7, the first term on the RHS satisfies

∑t=K+1T𝟙{Nt−1kt(β)≥A}⋅γT−t(μ~t−1kt⋆−μ~t−1kt)≤2​1+A−1​∑t=K+1TγT−t​rtkt≤4​∑t=K+1TγT−t​rtkt,\begin{aligned} \sum_{t=K+1}^{T}\mathbbm{1}\left\{N_{t-1}^{k_{t}}(\beta)\geq A\right\}\cdot\gamma^{T-t}\Bigl(\tilde{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}^{\star}}-\tilde{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}}\Bigr)&\leq 2\sqrt{1+A^{-1}}\sum_{t=K+1}^{T}\gamma^{T-t}r_{t}^{k_{t}}\\ &\leq 4\sum_{t=K+1}^{T}\gamma^{T-t}r_{t}^{k_{t}}\\ \end{aligned},

with probability at least 1−2​H​(β)−α1-2H(\beta)^{-\alpha}, where A−1≤3A^{-1}\leq 3 by construction. Thus it follows from a union bound that

Pr[∑t=K+1T𝟙{Nt−1kt(β)≥A}⋅γT−t(μ~t−1kt⋆−μ~t−1kt)≥4∑t=K+1TγT−trtkt]≤∑t=K+1TPr[μ~t−1kt⋆−μ~t−1kt≥4rtkt,Nt−1kt(β)≥A]≤2​T​H​(β)−α.\begin{aligned} \Pr&\left[\sum_{t=K+1}^{T}\mathbbm{1}\left\{N_{t-1}^{k_{t}}(\beta)\geq A\right\}\cdot\gamma^{T-t}\Bigl(\tilde{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}^{\star}}-\tilde{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}}\Bigr)\geq 4\sum_{t=K+1}^{T}\gamma^{T-t}r_{t}^{k_{t}}\right]\\ &\leq\sum_{t=K+1}^{T}\Pr\left[\tilde{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}^{\star}}-\tilde{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}}\geq 4r_{t}^{k_{t}},N_{t-1}^{k_{t}}(\beta)\geq A\right]\\ &\leq 2TH(\beta)^{-\alpha}\\ \end{aligned}.

By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, we have ∑k=1KNTk​(β)≤K​NT​(β)\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sqrt{N_{T}^{k}(\beta)}\leq\sqrt{KN_{T}(\beta)}. Thus

4​∑t=K+1TγT−t​rtkt=8​C​2​α​ln⁡H​(β)​∑t=K+1TγT−tNtk​(β)=8​C​2​α​ln⁡H​(β)​∑k=1K∑t=K+1T𝟙{kt=k}⋅γT−tNtk​(β)≤8​C​2​α​ln⁡H​(β)​∑k=1K(2​NTk​(β)12+NTk​(γ)​H​(β)−12)≤8​C​2​α​ln⁡H​(β)​(2​K12​NT​(β)12+NT​(γ)​H​(β)−12),\begin{aligned} 4\sum_{t=K+1}^{T}\gamma^{T-t}r_{t}^{k_{t}}&=8C\sqrt{2\alpha\ln H(\beta)}\sum_{t=K+1}^{T}\frac{\gamma^{T-t}}{\sqrt{N_{t}^{k}(\beta)}}\\ &=8C\sqrt{2\alpha\ln H(\beta)}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{t=K+1}^{T}\frac{\mathbbm{1}\left\{k_{t}=k\right\}\cdot\gamma^{T-t}}{\sqrt{N_{t}^{k}(\beta)}}\\ &\leq 8C\sqrt{2\alpha\ln H(\beta)}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\Bigl(2N_{T}^{k}(\beta)^{\frac{1}{2}}+N_{T}^{k}(\gamma)H(\beta)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\Bigr)\\ &\leq 8C\sqrt{2\alpha\ln H(\beta)}\bigl(2K^{\frac{1}{2}}N_{T}(\beta)^{\frac{1}{2}}+N_{T}(\gamma)H(\beta)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\bigr)\\ \end{aligned},

where the first inequality follows from Lemma 4. Further combining with Proposition 8, we have

∑t=K+1T𝟙{Nt−1kt(β)≥A}⋅γT−t(μ~t−1kt⋆−μ~t−1kt)≤8​C​2​α​ln⁡H​(β)​(2​K12​NT​(β)12+NT​(γ)​H​(β)−12)+2​η​G2​NT​(γ)​H​(β)​ln⁡(2​C​eη​A​G2),\begin{aligned} \sum_{t=K+1}^{T}\mathbbm{1}&\left\{N_{t-1}^{k_{t}}(\beta)\geq A\right\}\cdot\gamma^{T-t}\Bigl(\tilde{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}^{\star}}-\tilde{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}}\Bigr)\\ \leq&~8C\sqrt{2\alpha\ln H(\beta)}\bigl(2K^{\frac{1}{2}}N_{T}(\beta)^{\frac{1}{2}}+N_{T}(\gamma)H(\beta)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\bigr)\\ &~+2\eta G^{2}N_{T}(\gamma)H(\beta)\ln\left(\frac{2Ce}{\eta AG^{2}}\right)\\ \end{aligned},

with probability at least 2​T​H​(β)−α2TH(\beta)^{-\alpha}. And when the bound fails, the additional regret incurred is at most 2​C​T​NT​(γ)​H​(β)−α2CTN_{T}(\gamma)H(\beta)^{-\alpha}. Putting together,

𝔼⁡[Rbγ​(D−UCBT)]≤\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigl[R_{b}^{\gamma}(\operatorname{D-UCB}_{T})\bigr]\leq γT−K​C​K+4​A​C​K​(T​NT​(β)−1+1)\displaystyle\gamma^{T-K}CK+4ACK\bigl(TN_{T}(\beta)^{-1}+1\bigr)
+8​C​2​α​ln⁡H​(β)​(2​K12​NT​(β)12+NT​(γ)​H​(β)−12)\displaystyle+8C\sqrt{2\alpha\ln H(\beta)}\bigl(2K^{\frac{1}{2}}N_{T}(\beta)^{\frac{1}{2}}+N_{T}(\gamma)H(\beta)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\bigr)
+2​η​G2​NT​(γ)​H​(β)​ln⁡(2​C​eη​A​G2)\displaystyle+2\eta G^{2}N_{T}(\gamma)H(\beta)\ln\left(\frac{2Ce}{\eta AG^{2}}\right)
+2​C​NT​(γ)​H​(β)1−α\displaystyle+2CN_{T}(\gamma)H(\beta)^{1-\alpha}

Setting a sufficiently large α\alpha (e.g., α=(ln⁡T+ln⁡H⁡(γ))/ln⁡H⁡(β)\alpha=(\ln T+\ln H(\gamma))/\ln H(\beta) s.t. T​NT​(γ)​H​(β)1−α≤1TN_{T}(\gamma)H(\beta)^{1-\alpha}\leq 1) concludes the proof. ∎

Proposition 10 (Normalized Dynamic Bandit Regret of DUCB).

The normalized dynamic bandit regret of DUCB satisfies

TNT​(γ)​𝔼​[Rbγ​(DUCBT)]≤{O~​(K12​T12)η≤O⁡(T−23)O~​(η13​K13​T)O⁡(T−32)≤η≤o⁡(1)\frac{T}{N_{T}(\gamma)}\mathbb{E}\bigl[R_{b}^{\gamma}(\operatorname{DUCB}_{T})\bigr]\leq\begin{cases}\begin{aligned} &\tilde{O}\bigl(K^{\frac{1}{2}}T^{\frac{1}{2}}\bigr)&\eta\leq O(T^{-\frac{2}{3}})\\ &\tilde{O}\bigl(\eta^{\frac{1}{3}}K^{\frac{1}{3}}T\bigr)&O(T^{-\frac{3}{2}})\leq\eta\leq o(1)\\ \end{aligned}\end{cases}

for any γ∈[1−T−1,1]\gamma\in[1-T^{-1},1].

Proof.

First write

TNT​(γ)​𝔼​[Rbγ​(DUCBT)]≤O⁡(K​T2​NT​(γ)−1​H​(β)−1)+O~​(K12​T​NT​(γ)−1​H​(β)12)+O~​(T​H​(β)−12)+O~​(η​T​H​(β)).\begin{aligned} \frac{T}{N_{T}(\gamma)}\mathbb{E}\bigl[R_{b}^{\gamma}(\operatorname{DUCB}_{T})\bigr]\leq&~O\bigl(KT^{2}N_{T}(\gamma)^{-1}H(\beta)^{-1}\bigr)+\tilde{O}\bigl(K^{\frac{1}{2}}TN_{T}(\gamma)^{-1}H(\beta)^{\frac{1}{2}}\bigr)\\ &~+\tilde{O}\bigl(TH(\beta)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\bigr)+\tilde{O}\bigl(\eta TH(\beta)\bigr)\\ \end{aligned}.

Note that when γ≥1−T−1\gamma\geq 1-T^{-1}, we have

TNT​(γ)≤11−(1−T−1)T≤11−e−1≤2,\frac{T}{N_{T}(\gamma)}\leq\frac{1}{1-(1-T^{-1})^{T}}\leq\frac{1}{1-e^{-1}}\leq 2,

since (1−T−1)T↗e−1(1-T^{-1})^{T}\nearrow e^{-1} as T→∞T\to\infty. Then it follows that

TNT​(γ)​𝔼​[Rbγ​(DUCBT)]≤O⁡(K​T​H​(β)−1)+O~​(K12​H​(β)12)+O~​(T​H​(β)−12)+O~​(η​T​H​(β)).\begin{aligned} \frac{T}{N_{T}(\gamma)}\mathbb{E}\bigl[R_{b}^{\gamma}(\operatorname{DUCB}_{T})\bigr]\leq&~O\bigl(KTH(\beta)^{-1}\bigr)+\tilde{O}\bigl(K^{\frac{1}{2}}H(\beta)^{\frac{1}{2}}\bigr)\\ &~+\tilde{O}\bigl(TH(\beta)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\bigr)+\tilde{O}\bigl(\eta TH(\beta)\bigr)\\ \end{aligned}.

Now we discuss the choice of β\beta over different values of η\eta. When η≤o(T−3/2)\eta\leq o(T^{-{3/2}}), i.e., the environment is almost stationary, the last term is negligible since O⁡(η​T​H​(β))≤o⁡(T1/2)O(\eta TH(\beta))\leq o(T^{1/2}). Thus we can choose β=1−T−1\beta=1-T^{-1} s.t. H⁡(β)=TH(\beta)=T, and

TNT​(γ)​𝔼​[Rbγ​(DUCBT)]≤O⁡(K)+O~​(K12​T12)+O~​(T12)+o⁡(T12)=O~​(K12​T12).\begin{aligned} \frac{T}{N_{T}(\gamma)}\mathbb{E}\bigl[R_{b}^{\gamma}(\operatorname{DUCB}_{T})\bigr]&\leq O\bigl(K\bigr)+\tilde{O}\bigl(K^{\frac{1}{2}}T^{\frac{1}{2}}\bigr)+\tilde{O}\bigl(T^{\frac{1}{2}}\bigr)+o\bigl(T^{\frac{1}{2}}\bigr)\\ &=\tilde{O}\bigl(K^{\frac{1}{2}}T^{\frac{1}{2}}\bigr)\\ \end{aligned}.

When O(T−3/2)≤η≤o(1)O(T^{-3/2})\leq\eta\leq o(1), i.e., the environment is slowly changing, we have η​K≤1\eta K\leq 1 for any fixed KK independent of TT. Let β=1−η2/3K−1/3\beta=1-\eta^{2/3}K^{-1/3} s.t. H(β)=η−2/3K1/3H(\beta)=\eta^{-2/3}K^{1/3}. We have

TNT​(γ)​𝔼​[Rbγ​(DUCBT)]≤O⁡(η23​K23​T)+O~​(η13​K13)+O~​(η13​K−16​T)+O~​(η13​K13​T)=O~​(η13​K13​T).\begin{aligned} \frac{T}{N_{T}(\gamma)}\mathbb{E}\bigl[R_{b}^{\gamma}(\operatorname{DUCB}_{T})\bigr]&\leq O\bigl(\eta^{\frac{2}{3}}K^{\frac{2}{3}}T\bigr)+\tilde{O}\bigl(\eta^{\frac{1}{3}}K^{\frac{1}{3}}\bigr)+\tilde{O}\bigl(\eta^{\frac{1}{3}}K^{-\frac{1}{6}}T\bigr)+\tilde{O}\bigl(\eta^{\frac{1}{3}}K^{\frac{1}{3}}T\bigr)\\ &=\tilde{O}\bigl(\eta^{\frac{1}{3}}K^{\frac{1}{3}}T\bigr)\\ \end{aligned}.

Note that if η=O⁡(1)\eta=O(1), i.e., the environment is abruptly changing, no algorithm can achieve a sublinear regret given our setting where θt\theta_{t} changes in all steps Garivier and Moulines (2011). ∎

This proves Proposition 4.

C.4 Proof of Proposition 7

First we state a discounted version of Azuma’s inequality. Consider the sequence

{Ztk:=𝟙{kt=k}⋅(μ^k(θt;ℬt)−μk(θt)),t=1,…,T},k∈[K].\left\{Z_{t}^{k}:=\mathbbm{1}\left\{k_{t}=k\right\}\cdot\left(\hat{\mu}^{k}(\theta_{t};\mathcal{B}_{t})-\mu^{k}(\theta_{t})\right),t=1,\dots,T\right\},\quad k\in[K].

Note that θt\theta_{t} is σ⁡(𝒜t−1,𝒳t−1)\sigma(\mathcal{A}_{t-1},\mathcal{X}_{t-1})-measurable by the design of OGD. Further since

𝔼[Ztk|𝒜t−1,𝒳t−1]=𝔼[𝟙{kt=k}⋅(μ^k(θt;ℬt)−μk(θt))|θt]=Pr[kt=k]⋅(𝔼[μ^k(θt;ℬt)|kt,θt]−μk(θt))+Pr[kt≠k]⋅0=0,\begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}\left[Z_{t}^{k}\middle|\mathcal{A}_{t-1},\mathcal{X}_{t-1}\right]&=\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbbm{1}\left\{k_{t}=k\right\}\cdot\left(\hat{\mu}^{k}(\theta_{t};\mathcal{B}_{t})-\mu^{k}(\theta_{t})\right)\middle|\theta_{t}\right]\\ &=\Pr[k_{t}=k]\cdot\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\hat{\mu}^{k}(\theta_{t};\mathcal{B}_{t})\middle|k_{t},\theta_{t}\right]-\mu^{k}(\theta_{t})\right)+\Pr[k_{t}\neq k]\cdot 0\\ &=0\\ \end{aligned},

the sequence {Ztk,t=1,…,T}\{Z_{t}^{k},t=1,\dots,T\} is a martingale difference sequence for all fixed k∈[K]k\in[K]. We have the following lemma.

Proposition 11 (Discounted Azuma’s Inequality).

For any constant α>0\alpha>0 and β∈[0,1]\beta\in[0,1],

Pr[∑τ=1tβt−τZτk>2C(α+1)​Ntk​(β2)​ln⁡H⁡(β)]≤H(β)−α,\Pr\left[\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\beta^{t-\tau}Z_{\tau}^{k}>2C\sqrt{(\alpha+1)N_{t}^{k}(\beta^{2})\ln H(\beta)}\right]\leq H(\beta)^{-\alpha},

where Ntk​(⋅)N_{t}^{k}(\cdot) is defined in Eq. 7 and H⁡(⋅)H(\cdot) is defined in Eq. 8.

Proof.

The proof is an adaptation of the standard proof of Azuma’s inequality, where we specifically deal with the randomness of Ntk​(β2)N_{t}^{k}(\beta^{2}). Following Garivier and Moulines (2011), we apply a union bound over its possible values using the peeling technique. Specifically, let

M⁡(β,δ):=⌈ln⁡H⁡(β)ln⁡(1+δ)⌉,δ>0.M(\beta,\delta):=\left\lceil\frac{\ln H(\beta)}{\ln(1+\delta)}\right\rceil,\quad\delta>0.

Note that since 1−β≤ln⁡(1/β)≤1−1/β1-\beta\leq\ln(1/\beta)\leq 1-1/\beta, we have

β1−β≤H⁡(β)≤11−β.\frac{\beta}{1-\beta}\leq H(\beta)\leq\frac{1}{1-\beta}.

Define the intervals Im:=(nm−1,nm]I_{m}:=(n_{m-1},n_{m}] for each m∈[M⁡(β,δ)]m\in[M(\beta,\delta)], where we set n0:=0n_{0}:=0 and nm:=(1+δ)mn_{m}:=(1+\delta)^{m}. Then

nM=(1+δ)M⁡(β,δ)≥H⁡(β)=11−β≥11−β2≥Ntk​(β2),n_{M}=(1+\delta)^{M(\beta,\delta)}\geq H(\beta)=\frac{1}{1-\beta}\geq\frac{1}{1-\beta^{2}}\geq N_{t}^{k}(\beta^{2}),

and there exists a unique m∈[M⁡(β,δ)]m\in[M(\beta,\delta)] s.t. Ntk​(β2)∈ImN_{t}^{k}(\beta^{2})\in I_{m}. Then for any ϵ>0\epsilon>0,

Pr[∑τ=1tβt−τZτk>ϵ]=∑m=1M⁡(β,δ)Pr[∑τ=1tβt−τZτk>ϵ,Ntk(β2)∈Im].\Pr\left[\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\beta^{t-\tau}Z_{\tau}^{k}>\epsilon\right]=\sum_{m=1}^{M(\beta,\delta)}\Pr\left[\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\beta^{t-\tau}Z_{\tau}^{k}>\epsilon,N_{t}^{k}(\beta^{2})\in I_{m}\right].

For each event where Ntk​(β)∈ImN_{t}^{k}(\beta)\in I_{m}, there is Ntk​(β2)≤nmN_{t}^{k}(\beta^{2})\leq n_{m}, and thus

Pr[∑τ=1tβt−τZτk>ϵ,Ntk(β2)∈Im]≤Pr[∑τ=1tβt−τZτk−λ​C22Ntk(β2)>ϵ−λ​C22nm].\Pr\left[\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\beta^{t-\tau}Z_{\tau}^{k}>\epsilon,N_{t}^{k}(\beta^{2})\in I_{m}\right]\leq\Pr\left[\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\beta^{t-\tau}Z_{\tau}^{k}-\frac{\lambda C^{2}}{2}N_{t}^{k}(\beta^{2})>\epsilon-\frac{\lambda C^{2}}{2}n_{m}\right].

Then applying Chernoff’s bound to the RHS gives

Pr[∑τ=1tγt−τZτk>ϵ,Ntk(β2)∈Im]≤infλ>0exp⁡(−λ​ϵ+λ2​C22​nm)​𝔼​[exp⁡(λ​∑τ=1tγt−τ​Zτk−λ2​C22​Ntk​(β2))].\begin{aligned} \Pr&\left[\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\gamma^{t-\tau}Z_{\tau}^{k}>\epsilon,N_{t}^{k}(\beta^{2})\in I_{m}\right]\\ &\leq\inf_{\lambda>0}~\exp\left(-\lambda\epsilon+\frac{\lambda^{2}C^{2}}{2}n_{m}\right)\mathbb{E}\left[\exp\left(\lambda\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\gamma^{t-\tau}Z_{\tau}^{k}-\frac{\lambda^{2}C^{2}}{2}N_{t}^{k}(\beta^{2})\right)\right]\\ \end{aligned}.

Recall by Hoeffding’s lemma that

𝔼[exp(λβt−τZτk)|𝒜τ,𝒳τ−1]≤exp(𝟙{kτ=k}⋅λ2​β2​(t−τ)​C22).\mathbb{E}\left[\exp(\lambda\beta^{t-\tau}Z_{\tau}^{k})|\mathcal{A}_{\tau},\mathcal{X}_{\tau-1}\right]\leq\exp\left(\mathbbm{1}\left\{k_{\tau}=k\right\}\cdot\frac{\lambda^{2}\beta^{2(t-\tau)}C^{2}}{2}\right).

Then

𝔼[exp⁡(λ​∑τ=1tβt−τ​Zτk−λ2​C22​Ntk​(β2))]=𝔼[exp(λ∑τ=1t−1βt−τZτk−λ2​C22Ntk(β2))𝔼[exp(λZtk)|𝒜t,𝒳t−1]]≤𝔼[exp(λ∑τ=1t−1βt−τZτk−λ2​C22Ntk(β2))⋅exp(𝟙{kt=k}⋅λ2​C22)]≤…≤𝔼[exp(−λ2​C22Ntk(β2)+λ2​C22∑τ=1t𝟙{kτ=k}⋅β2​(t−τ))]=1.\begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}&\left[\exp\left(\lambda\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\beta^{t-\tau}Z_{\tau}^{k}-\frac{\lambda^{2}C^{2}}{2}N_{t}^{k}(\beta^{2})\right)\right]\\ &=\mathbb{E}\left[\exp\left(\lambda\sum_{\tau=1}^{t-1}\beta^{t-\tau}Z_{\tau}^{k}-\frac{\lambda^{2}C^{2}}{2}N_{t}^{k}(\beta^{2})\right)\mathbb{E}\left[\exp(\lambda Z_{t}^{k})\middle|\mathcal{A}_{t},\mathcal{X}_{t-1}\right]\right]\\ &\leq\mathbb{E}\left[\exp\left(\lambda\sum_{\tau=1}^{t-1}\beta^{t-\tau}Z_{\tau}^{k}-\frac{\lambda^{2}C^{2}}{2}N_{t}^{k}(\beta^{2})\right)\cdot\exp\left(\mathbbm{1}\left\{k_{t}=k\right\}\cdot\frac{\lambda^{2}C^{2}}{2}\right)\right]\\ &\leq\dots\\ &\leq\mathbb{E}\left[\exp\left(-\frac{\lambda^{2}C^{2}}{2}N_{t}^{k}(\beta^{2})+\frac{\lambda^{2}C^{2}}{2}\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\mathbbm{1}\left\{k_{\tau}=k\right\}\cdot\beta^{2(t-\tau)}\right)\right]\\ &=1\\ \end{aligned}.

Therefore,

Pr[∑τ=1tβt−τZτk>ϵ,Ntk(β2)∈Im]≤infλ>0exp(−λϵ+λ2​C22nm)=exp(−ϵ22​C2​nm),\Pr\left[\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\beta^{t-\tau}Z_{\tau}^{k}>\epsilon,N_{t}^{k}(\beta^{2})\in I_{m}\right]\leq\inf_{\lambda>0}~\exp\left(-\lambda\epsilon+\frac{\lambda^{2}C^{2}}{2}n_{m}\right)=\exp\left(-\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{2C^{2}n_{m}}\right),

where the RHS of the inequality is minimized by taking λ=ϵ/(C2​nm)\lambda=\epsilon/(C^{2}n_{m}). Since nm≤(1+δ)​Ntk​(β2)n_{m}\leq(1+\delta)N_{t}^{k}(\beta^{2}) for any Ntk​(β2)∈ImN_{t}^{k}(\beta^{2})\in I_{m}, we have

Pr[∑τ=1tβt−τZτk>C2​(1+δ)​Ntk​(β2)​ln⁡M⁡(β,δ)H​(β)−α,Ntk(β2)∈Im]≤Pr[∑τ=1tβt−τZτk>C2​nm​ln⁡M⁡(β,δ)H​(β)−α,Ntk(β2)∈Im]≤H​(β)−αM⁡(β,δ).\begin{aligned} \Pr&\left[\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\beta^{t-\tau}Z_{\tau}^{k}>C\sqrt{2(1+\delta)N_{t}^{k}(\beta^{2})\ln\frac{M(\beta,\delta)}{H(\beta)^{-\alpha}}},N_{t}^{k}(\beta^{2})\in I_{m}\right]\\ &\leq\Pr\left[\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\beta^{t-\tau}Z_{\tau}^{k}>C\sqrt{2n_{m}\ln\frac{M(\beta,\delta)}{H(\beta)^{-\alpha}}},N_{t}^{k}(\beta^{2})\in I_{m}\right]\\ &\leq\frac{H(\beta)^{-\alpha}}{M(\beta,\delta)}\\ \end{aligned}.

Combining together, we have

Pr[∑τ=1tβt−τZτk>C2​(1+δ)​Ntk​(β2)​ln⁡M⁡(β,δ)H​(β)−α]≤H(β)−α.\Pr\left[\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\beta^{t-\tau}Z_{\tau}^{k}>C\sqrt{2(1+\delta)N_{t}^{k}(\beta^{2})\ln\frac{M(\beta,\delta)}{H(\beta)^{-\alpha}}}\right]\leq H(\beta)^{-\alpha}.

Finally, we choose δ>0\delta>0 s.t. M⁡(β,δ)=H⁡(β)M(\beta,\delta)=H(\beta), i.e., as β→1\beta\to 1,

1+δ=H​(β)1/H⁡(β)↗e1e<2.1+\delta=H(\beta)^{1/H(\beta)}\nearrow e^{\frac{1}{e}}<2.

This concludes the proof. ∎

Then we immediately have the following result.

Lemma 5.

For any α≥1\alpha\geq 1,

Pr[μ^tk−μ~tk>2C2​α​ln⁡H​(β)Ntk​(β)]≤H(β)−α.\Pr\left[\hat{\mu}_{t}^{k}-\tilde{\mu}_{t}^{k}>2C\sqrt{\frac{2\alpha\ln H(\beta)}{N_{t}^{k}(\beta)}}\right]\leq H(\beta)^{-\alpha}.
Proof.

Note that

μ^tk−μ~tk=1Ntk​(γ)​∑τ=1tγt−τ​Zτk.\hat{\mu}_{t}^{k}-\tilde{\mu}_{t}^{k}=\frac{1}{N_{t}^{k}(\gamma)}\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\gamma^{t-\tau}Z_{\tau}^{k}.

Since Ntk​(γ)≥Ntk​(γ2)N_{t}^{k}(\gamma)\geq N_{t}^{k}(\gamma^{2}) for all γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1), we have

CNtk​(γ)​(α+1)​Ntk​(γ2)​ln⁡H⁡(γ)≤C​(α+1)​ln⁡H​(γ)Ntk​(γ)≤C​2​α​ln⁡H​(γ)Ntk​(γ),\frac{C}{N_{t}^{k}(\gamma)}\sqrt{(\alpha+1)N_{t}^{k}(\gamma^{2})\ln H(\gamma)}\leq C\sqrt{\frac{(\alpha+1)\ln H(\gamma)}{N_{t}^{k}(\gamma)}}\leq C\sqrt{\frac{2\alpha\ln H(\gamma)}{N_{t}^{k}(\gamma)}},

for all α≥1\alpha\geq 1. Then

Pr[μ^tk−μ~tk>2C2​α​ln⁡H​(γ)Ntk​(γ)]≤Pr[∑τ=1tγt−τZτk>2C(α+1)​Ntk​(γ)​ln⁡H⁡(γ)]≤H​(γ)−α,\begin{aligned} \Pr\left[\hat{\mu}_{t}^{k}-\tilde{\mu}_{t}^{k}>2C\sqrt{\frac{2\alpha\ln H(\gamma)}{N_{t}^{k}(\gamma)}}\right]&\leq\Pr\left[\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\gamma^{t-\tau}Z_{\tau}^{k}>2C\sqrt{(\alpha+1)N_{t}^{k}(\gamma)\ln H(\gamma)}\right]\\ &\leq H(\gamma)^{-\alpha}\\ \end{aligned},

where the last inequality follows from Proposition 11. ∎

Now we can prove the DUCB bandit gap.

Proof of Proposition 7.

By the rule of DUCB,

μ^t−1k+rt−1k≤μ^t−1kt+rt−1kt,∀k∈[K].\hat{\mu}_{t-1}^{k}+r_{t-1}^{k}\leq\hat{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}}+r_{t-1}^{k_{t}},\quad\forall k\in[K].

Specifically for k=kt⋆k=k_{t}^{\star}, there is

Δ^t−1kt:=μ^t−1kt⋆−μ^t−1kt≤rt−1kt−rt−1kt⋆.\hat{\Delta}_{t-1}^{k_{t}}:=\hat{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}^{\star}}-\hat{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}}\leq r_{t-1}^{k_{t}}-r_{t-1}^{k_{t}^{\star}}.

When Nt−1k​(β)≥AN_{t-1}^{k}(\beta)\geq A, we have

1+A−1Nt​(β)=Nt−1k​(β)+A−1​Nt−1k​(β)Nt−1k​(β)​Nt​(β)≥Nt−1k​(β)+1Nt−1k​(β)​Nt​(β)≥1Nt−1k​(β),\frac{1+A^{-1}}{N_{t}(\beta)}=\frac{N_{t-1}^{k}(\beta)+A^{-1}N_{t-1}^{k}(\beta)}{N_{t-1}^{k}(\beta)N_{t}(\beta)}\geq\frac{N_{t-1}^{k}(\beta)+1}{N_{t-1}^{k}(\beta)N_{t}(\beta)}\geq\frac{1}{N_{t-1}^{k}(\beta)},

where the last inequality is due to Nt−1k​(β)+1≥Ntk​(β)N_{t-1}^{k}(\beta)+1\geq N_{t}^{k}(\beta). Thus

rtk​1+A−1=2​C​1+A−1Ntk​(β)⋅2​α​ln⁡H​(β)≥2​C​2​α​ln⁡H​(β)Nt−1k​(β)=rt−1k.r_{t}^{k}\sqrt{1+A^{-1}}=2C\sqrt{\frac{1+A^{-1}}{N_{t}^{k}(\beta)}\cdot 2\alpha\ln H(\beta)}\geq 2C\sqrt{\frac{2\alpha\ln H(\beta)}{N_{t-1}^{k}(\beta)}}=r_{t-1}^{k}.

Then by the standard UCB argument,

Pr[μ~t−1kt⋆−μ~t−1kt>2rtkt1+A−1,Nt−1kt(β)≥A]≤Pr[μ~t−1kt⋆−μ~t−1kt>2rt−1kt]=Pr[μ~t−1kt⋆−μ~t−1kt−Δ^t−1kt>2rt−1kt−Δ^t−1kt]≤Pr[(μ~t−1kt⋆−μ^t−1kt⋆)−(μ~t−1kt−μ^t−1kt)>rt−1kt⋆+rt−1kt]≤Pr[μ^t−1kt⋆−μ~t−1kt⋆<−rt−1kt⋆]+Pr[μ^t−1kt−μ~t−1kt>rt−1kt].\begin{aligned} \Pr&\left[\tilde{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}^{\star}}-\tilde{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}}>2r_{t}^{k_{t}}\sqrt{1+A^{-1}},N_{t-1}^{k_{t}}(\beta)\geq A\right]\\ &\leq\Pr\left[\tilde{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}^{\star}}-\tilde{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}}>2r_{t-1}^{k_{t}}\right]\\ &=\Pr\left[\tilde{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}^{\star}}-\tilde{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}}-\hat{\Delta}_{t-1}^{k_{t}}>2r_{t-1}^{k_{t}}-\hat{\Delta}_{t-1}^{k_{t}}\right]\\ &\leq\Pr\left[\bigl(\tilde{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}^{\star}}-\hat{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}^{\star}}\bigr)-\bigl(\tilde{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}}-\hat{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}}\bigr)>r_{t-1}^{k_{t}^{\star}}+r_{t-1}^{k_{t}}\right]\\ &\leq\Pr\Bigl[\hat{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}^{\star}}-\tilde{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}^{\star}}<-r_{t-1}^{k_{t}^{\star}}\Bigr]+\Pr\Bigl[\hat{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}}-\tilde{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}}>r_{t-1}^{k_{t}}\Bigr]\\ \end{aligned}.

Applying Lemma 5 respectively on each term concludes the proof. ∎

C.5 Proof of Proposition 8

We prove this by splitting the EMA summands by a horizon D⁡(β)D(\beta) at each step tt. Note that the early summands for τ=1,…,⌊D⁡(β)⌋\tau=1,\dots,\lfloor{D(\beta)}\rfloor inherits more bias, since they are calculated based on some model parameter drastically different from the current parameter θt\theta_{t}. Thus we simply apply the boundedness condition. On the other hand, more recent summands for τ=⌈D⁡(β)⌉,…,t\tau=\lceil{D(\beta)}\rceil,\dots,t are calculated based on the model parameters much closer to the current θt\theta_{t}. Thus we bound them using the Lipschitz condition in Assumption 2. Finally, we optimize the choice of D⁡(β)D(\beta) to obtain Proposition 8.

Proof of Proposition 8.

Suppose there exists some 0≤D⁡(β)≤t0\leq D(\beta)\leq t for t∈[T]t\in[T]. We can write

|μ~tk−μk​(θt+1)|=1Ntk​(β)|∑τ=1t𝟙{kτ=k}⋅βt−τ(μk(θτ)−μk(θt+1))|≤1Ntk​(β)|∑τ=1t−⌊D⁡(β)⌋𝟙{kτ=k}⋅βt−τ(μk(θτ)−μk(θt+1))|+1Ntk​(β)|∑τ=t−⌈D⁡(β)⌉t𝟙{kτ=k}⋅βt−τ(μk(θτ)−μk(θt+1))|.\begin{aligned} \left|\tilde{\mu}_{t}^{k}-\mu^{k}(\theta_{t+1})\right|=&~\frac{1}{N_{t}^{k}(\beta)}\left|\sum_{\tau=1}^{t}\mathbbm{1}\left\{k_{\tau}=k\right\}\cdot\beta^{t-\tau}\left(\mu^{k}(\theta_{\tau})-\mu^{k}(\theta_{t+1})\right)\right|\\ \leq&~\frac{1}{N_{t}^{k}(\beta)}\left|\sum_{\tau=1}^{t-\lfloor D(\beta)\rfloor}\mathbbm{1}\left\{k_{\tau}=k\right\}\cdot\beta^{t-\tau}\left(\mu^{k}(\theta_{\tau})-\mu^{k}(\theta_{t+1})\right)\right|\\ &~+\frac{1}{N_{t}^{k}(\beta)}\left|\sum_{\tau=t-\lceil D(\beta)\rceil}^{t}\mathbbm{1}\left\{k_{\tau}=k\right\}\cdot\beta^{t-\tau}\left(\mu^{k}(\theta_{\tau})-\mu^{k}(\theta_{t+1})\right)\right|\\ \end{aligned}.

For the first sum, since |μk​(θτ)−μk​(θt)|<C|\mu^{k}(\theta_{\tau})-\mu^{k}(\theta_{t})|<C for all τ,t∈[T]\tau,t\in[T], we have

1Ntk​(β)|∑τ=1t−⌊D⁡(β)⌋𝟙{kt=k}⋅βt−τ(μk(θτ)−μk(θt+1))|≤C​β⌊D⁡(β)⌋Ntk​(β)∑τ=1t−⌊D⁡(β)⌋𝟙{kτ=k}⋅βt−⌊D⁡(β)⌋−τ=C​βD⁡(β)​Nt−⌊D⁡(β)⌋k​(β)Ntk​(β)≤C​A−1​H​(β)​βD⁡(β).\begin{aligned} \frac{1}{N_{t}^{k}(\beta)}&\left|\sum_{\tau=1}^{t-\lfloor D(\beta)\rfloor}\mathbbm{1}\left\{k_{t}=k\right\}\cdot\beta^{t-\tau}\left(\mu^{k}(\theta_{\tau})-\mu^{k}(\theta_{t+1})\right)\right|\\ &\leq\frac{C\beta^{\lfloor D(\beta)\rfloor}}{N_{t}^{k}(\beta)}\sum_{\tau=1}^{t-\lfloor D(\beta)\rfloor}\mathbbm{1}\left\{k_{\tau}=k\right\}\cdot\beta^{t-\lfloor D(\beta)\rfloor-\tau}\\ &=\frac{C\beta^{D(\beta)}N_{t-\lfloor D(\beta)\rfloor}^{k}(\beta)}{N_{t}^{k}(\beta)}\\ &\leq CA^{-1}H(\beta)\beta^{D(\beta)}\\ \end{aligned}.

For the second sum, by the Lipschitz condition and the rule of OGD, we have

maxτ∈[t−⌈D⁡(β)⌉,t]⁡|μk​(θτ)−μk​(θt+1)|≤G‖∑τ=t−⌈D⁡(β)⌉tη∇μ^kt(θτ;⋅)‖≤η​G2​D​(β).\begin{aligned} \max_{\tau\in[t-\lceil D(\beta)\rceil,t]}~\left|\mu^{k}(\theta_{\tau})-\mu^{k}(\theta_{t+1})\right|&\leq G\left\|\sum_{\tau=t-\lceil D(\beta)\rceil}^{t}\eta\nabla\hat{\mu}^{k_{t}}(\theta_{\tau};\cdot)\right\|\\ &\leq\eta G^{2}D(\beta)\\ \end{aligned}.

Then

|μ~tk−μk​(θt+1)|≤C​A−1​H​(β)​βD⁡(β)+η​G2​D​(β).\left|\tilde{\mu}_{t}^{k}-\mu^{k}(\theta_{t+1})\right|\leq CA^{-1}H(\beta)\beta^{D(\beta)}+\eta G^{2}D(\beta).

To choose the optimal D⁡(β)D(\beta), let

dd​D​(β)​|μ~tk−μk​(θt+1)|=C​A−1​H​(β)​(ln⁡β)​βD⁡(β)+η​G2=0,\frac{d}{dD(\beta)}\left|\tilde{\mu}_{t}^{k}-\mu^{k}(\theta_{t+1})\right|=CA^{-1}H(\beta)(\ln\beta)\beta^{D(\beta)}+\eta G^{2}=0,

i.e.,

D⋆​(β)=1ln⁡β​ln⁡(η​A​G2C​H​(β)​ln⁡(1/β)).D^{\star}(\beta)=\frac{1}{\ln\beta}\ln\left(\frac{\eta AG^{2}}{CH(\beta)\ln(1/\beta)}\right).

Further note that the LHS is convex in D⁡(β)D(\beta). Thus the assumption that 0≤D⁡(β)≤t0\leq D(\beta)\leq t can be alleviated, and

|μ~tk−μk​(θt+1)|≤η​G2ln⁡(1/β)​(1+ln⁡(C​H​(β)​ln⁡(1/β)η​A​G2)).\left|\tilde{\mu}_{t}^{k}-\mu^{k}(\theta_{t+1})\right|\leq\frac{\eta G^{2}}{\ln(1/\beta)}\left(1+\ln\left(\frac{CH(\beta)\ln(1/\beta)}{\eta AG^{2}}\right)\right).

Finally, since ln⁡(1/β)≥1−β=H​(β)−1\ln(1/\beta)\geq 1-\beta=H(\beta)^{-1}, we conclude the proof by realizing that the RHS above is monotonically decreasing w.r.t. ln⁡(1/β)\ln(1/\beta), and H⁡(β)​ln⁡(1/β)≤1/β≤2H(\beta)\ln(1/\beta)\leq 1/\beta\leq 2 for all β≥1/2\beta\geq 1/2. ∎

C.6 Analysis of Sampling DUCB

To show that the bandit regret of the sampling version of DUCB is a constant factor away from the standard DUCB, we only need to show that the bandit gap is a constant factor away from Proposition 7, and the rest naturally follows.

Proposition 12 (Bandit Gap of Sampling DUCB).

Suppose sampling DUCB picks ktk_{t} in step t≥K+1t\geq K+1 as in appendix B. Then for any A>0A>0,

Pr[μ~t−1kt⋆−μ~t−1kt>4rtkt1+A−1,Nt−1kt(β)≥A]≤4H(β)−α.\Pr\left[\tilde{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}^{\star}}-\tilde{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}}>4r_{t}^{k_{t}}\sqrt{1+A^{-1}},N_{t-1}^{k_{t}}(\beta)\geq A\right]\leq 4H(\beta)^{-\alpha}.
Proof.

By the rule of sampling DUCB, we have

μ^t−1k+ϕt−1k≤μ^t−1kt+ϕt−1kt,∀k∈[K].\hat{\mu}_{t-1}^{k}+\phi_{t-1}^{k}\leq\hat{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}}+\phi_{t-1}^{k_{t}},\quad\forall k\in[K].

And specifically for k=kt⋆k=k_{t}^{\star} (recall that kt⋆=arg​maxk⁡μk​(θt)k_{t}^{\star}=\argmax_{k}\mu^{k}(\theta_{t})),

Δ^tkt=μ^t−1kt⋆−μ^t−1kt≤ϕt−1kt−ϕt−1kt⋆.\hat{\Delta}_{t}^{k_{t}}=\hat{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}^{\star}}-\hat{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}}\leq\phi_{t-1}^{k_{t}}-\phi_{t-1}^{k_{t}^{\star}}.

According to the Gaussian tail bound,

Pr[ϕt−1k−2rt−1k>rt−1k]≤H(β)−α,Pr[ϕt−1k−2rt−1k<−rt−1k]≤H(β)−α.\Pr\left[\phi_{t-1}^{k}-2r_{t-1}^{k}>r_{t-1}^{k}\right]\leq H(\beta)^{-\alpha},\quad\Pr\left[\phi_{t-1}^{k}-2r_{t-1}^{k}<-r_{t-1}^{k}\right]\leq H(\beta)^{-\alpha}.

Recall by Proposition 7 that (1+A−1)​Ntk​(β)−1≥Nt−1k​(β)−1(1+A^{-1})N_{t}^{k}(\beta)^{-1}\geq N_{t-1}^{k}(\beta)^{-1}. Then

Pr[μ~t−1kt⋆−μ~t−1kt>4rtkt1+A−1,Nt−1kt(β)≥A]≤Pr[μ~t−1kt⋆−μ~t−1kt>4rt−1kt]=Pr[μ~t−1kt⋆−μ~t−1kt−Δ^tkt+Δ^tkt>4rt−1kt]≤Pr[(μ~t−1kt⋆−μ^t−1kt⋆)−(μ~t−1kt−μ^t−1kt)+ϕt−1kt−ϕt−1kt⋆>4rt−1kt+rt−1kt⋆−rt−1kt⋆]≤Pr[μ^t−1kt⋆−μ~t−1kt⋆<−rt−1kt⋆]+Pr[μ^t−1kt−μ~t−1kt(θt)>rt−1kt]+Pr[ϕt−1kt>3rt−1kt]+Pr[ϕt−1kt⋆<rt−1kt⋆],\begin{aligned} \Pr&\left[\tilde{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}^{\star}}-\tilde{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}}>4r_{t}^{k_{t}}\sqrt{1+A^{-1}},N_{t-1}^{k_{t}}(\beta)\geq A\right]\\ &\leq\Pr\left[\tilde{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}^{\star}}-\tilde{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}}>4r_{t-1}^{k_{t}}\right]\\ &=\Pr\left[\tilde{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}^{\star}}-\tilde{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}}-\hat{\Delta}_{t}^{k_{t}}+\hat{\Delta}_{t}^{k_{t}}>4r_{t-1}^{k_{t}}\right]\\ &\leq\Pr\left[\bigl(\tilde{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}^{\star}}-\hat{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}^{\star}}\bigr)-\bigl(\tilde{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}}-\hat{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}}\bigr)+\phi_{t-1}^{k_{t}}-\phi_{t-1}^{k_{t}^{\star}}>4r_{t-1}^{k_{t}}+r_{t-1}^{k_{t}^{\star}}-r_{t-1}^{k_{t}^{\star}}\right]\\ &\leq\Pr\Bigl[\hat{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}^{\star}}-\tilde{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}^{\star}}<-r_{t-1}^{k_{t}^{\star}}\Bigr]+\Pr\Bigl[\hat{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}}-\tilde{\mu}_{t-1}^{k_{t}}(\theta_{t})>r_{t-1}^{k_{t}}\Bigr]\\ &~~~~+\Pr\Bigl[\phi_{t-1}^{k_{t}}>3r_{t-1}^{k_{t}}\Bigr]+\Pr\Bigl[\phi_{t-1}^{k_{t}^{\star}}<r_{t-1}^{k_{t}^{\star}}\Bigr]\\ \end{aligned},

where the last inequality follows from a union bound. Applying Lemma 5 and the Gaussian tail bound respectively on each term concludes the proof. ∎

Appendix D Additional Experimental Results

This section provides additional results beyond the compact Tab. 2. The goal is two-fold. First, we evaluate whether the behavior of DUCB transfers across model families and parameter scales. Second, we report auxiliary metrics, including mean token accuracy for SFT and reward margin for DPO, to verify that improvements in the primary robustness metric do not arise from degenerate behavior on secondary measures.

All models are trained either on a single 80G or two 40G NVIDIA A100 GPU(s), using the AdamW optimizer with 8-bit LoRA quantization and bfloat-16 mixed precision. The training was conducted using the NSF COSMOS Testbed (Raychaudhuri et al., 2020) and the Empire AI (Bloom et al., 2025) resources. For each set of experiments, we set a uniform sample budget and explicitly avoid training for multiple epochs. The goal is to ensure that every training mini-batch is non-repetitive and aligns with Assumption 3. Detailed configurations and scripts will be released with the code upon publication.

D.1 SFT

We evaluate the SFT performance on a heterogeneous dataset comprising GSM8k Cobbe et al. (2021) and IFEval Zhou et al. (2023), evaluating the model’s ability to balance mathematical reasoning with instruction-following. We compare against Exp3 utilizing standard SFT loss and the DynamixSFT-style stepwise loss difference proposed by Shin et al. (2025). We approximate their forward anticipated loss probing using virtual parameter update (followed parameter reset) with backward observed loss subtraction.

The observations confirm that DUCB consistently fulfills its theoretical promise of robustness, achieving the highest minimum source-wise across all model architectures and sizes. Note that the DynamixSFT-style proxy tends to achieve higher average accuracy, which aligns with their goal of optimizing the average performance.

D.2 DPO

We evaluate the DPO performance on the HelpSteer3 Wang et al. (2025c); Wang et al. (2025e) dataset in Tab. 4. We compare against compare against faithful implementations of AutoMixAlign Corrado et al. (2025) including both AMA-R and AMA-S, and Exp3-style samplers based on excess loss. Specifically, we train the model using uniform sampling for 100 steps, and utilize the (smoothed) training loss as a proxy to the loss of a specialist model for each data source. Then we use the difference between the instantaneous training losses and the specialist loss proxies as the Exp3 sampling signal. Additionally, we also compare against a fixed weight sampler, which assigns a deterministic weight based on the specialist loss proxies for each model, respectively.

The results reveal that DUCB outperforms AMA-R on both models and remains competitive with AMA-S, which achieves higher minimum accuracy on Qwen2.5-3B. It is also worth noting that the simple fixed-weight sampler performs exceptionally well for Llama3.2-3B, while failing to beat the uniform sampling baseline for Qwen2.5-3B. This suggests that a relatively stationary data mixture method is not uniformly applicable for all model families without case-specific tunings. On the other hand, DUCB demonstrates its capacity to automatically detect and adapt to these varying levels of non-stationarity.

We further evaluate the performance of Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct on the Helpsteer3 dataset over three random seeds. Under the original sample budget, hyperparameters, and evaluation protocol, DUCB outperforms Uniform in minimum accuracy in all three matched Qwen2.5-3B DPO runs. As shown in Tab. 5, DUCB improves the final-checkpoint minimum accuracy by 2.57±\pm1.04 percentage points while exhibiting lower variation across seeds. This provides controlled seed-level evidence of improved worst-source robustness without relying on aggregation across different datasets or model families.

D.3 GRPO

We evaluate GRPO under a broader set of model families, scales, and sampling signals inpired by different baselines. Specifically, Ramesh et al. (2026) utilize Exp3 guided by training reward with stepwise reward improvement correction; Wang et al. (2025b) adopt switching-window UCB (SWUCB) guided by training advantages. We focus on the Reasoning Chollet (2019); Katz et al. (2025); Lin et al. (2025) dataset and the CommonsenseQA Talmor et al. (2019) dataset.

For Reasoning shown in Tab. 6, DUCB consistently provides the strongest robustness guarantees, achieving the highest minimum source-wise accuracies across all tested models. For CommonsenseQA shown in Tab. 7, DUCB achieves the best or tied-best minimum source-wise accuracy across all four models. This suggests that the robustness of DUCB is not tied to a specific architecture, tokenizer, or pretraining recipe.

The comparison with Exp3-style Ramesh et al. (2026) and DUMP Wang et al. (2025b) baselines further highlights the importance of using a sampling signal aligned with worst-source robustness. Specifically, samplers that are based on reward difference or advantage does not consistently improve worst-source accuracy, affirming the findings of Ramesh et al. (2026). We also observe that the gains are comparably clearer on the smaller models, indicating that they may be more vulnerable to source-wise imbalance during GRPO. On the other hand, larger models may already possess stronger prior knowledge and thus exhibit more robustness.

D.4 Training Overhead

We measure per-step runtime on the same A100 GPU using the three Qwen2.5-3B DPO runs. DUCB requires 21.94±1.1421.94\pm 1.14 seconds per step, compared with 21.90±1.2921.90\pm 1.29 for Uniform, with the difference falling within the observed variations. DUCB uses losses already computed during optimization, adds no auxiliary model evaluations, and maintains only O⁡(K)O(K) scalar state. The generalist-training runtimes of AMA-R and AMA-S are similarly close to Uniform, but exclude their additional cost of training KK source-specific specialists. By contrast, the oracle of Zang et al. (2025) re-evaluates a growing history of collected samples under the current model. Thus, DUCB introduces little measurable online overhead while avoiding both auxiliary specialist training and replay-based model evaluations.

D.5 Optimization Dynamics and Assumption Diagnostics

Lipschitz regularity with respect to model parameters is commonly adopted in theoretical analyses of LLM optimization (Malladi et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2025). In our analysis, its primary role is to control changes in source losses between successive iterates visited by the optimization trajectory; we do not characterize a global Lipschitz constant for a transformer over its entire parameter space. We interpret Assumption 2 accordingly as a trajectory-level regularity condition.

In practice, small learning rates, gradient clipping, learning-rate schedules, and, where applicable, KL regularization help control parameter updates during LLM post-training. To examine whether the slowly varying loss environment assumed by our analysis is representative of our experiments, we record the learning rate and gradient norm reported by TRL or veRL, together with the maximum absolute change in each source’s exponentially smoothed training signal between consecutive steps. We also report the frequency with which the empirically worst source changes during training.

As shown in Tab. 9, the experiments use maximum learning rates of at most 2×10−52\times 10^{-5}, and the observed source-wise training signals change modestly between consecutive steps. At the same time, the identity of the worst source changes repeatedly across all three objectives, indicating a slowly varying but nonstationary environment. These observations are consistent with the trajectory-level regularity and slow-variation assumptions used in our analysis. They do not prove global Lipschitzness or estimate a global Lipschitz constant for the underlying neural networks.
